speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
He said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise on second reading of Bill C-110, which will create the Canadian International Trade Tribunal and consequently amend and repeal a number of other Acts. The Canadien International Trade Tribunal will replace and take over the functions of the three institutions: the Canadian Import Tribunal, the Textile and Clothing Board and the Tariff Board. The legislation creating these latter institutions will be repealed and they will disappear. The Bill also contains amendments to other Acts. These amendments are consequential to the Bill and technical in nature. The Bill also includes provisions to ensure an orderly transition to the new tribunal.
The decision in principle to amalgamate the three import institutions was first announced in the May 1985 budget. This is part of the Government's efforts to rationalize and streamline federal institutions and practices. By bringing the functions of these institutions under one roof, expertise and knowledge regarding trade matters will be more efficiently focused. The treatment of import and other international trade issues will be harmonized. The new tribunal will provide a central and common focus for examining the trade-related concerns of Canadians. The Government will have a sound and consistent base on which to make decisions.
The easiest way to explain the main purpose of Bill C-l 10 is to first look at the responsibilities of the existing three institutions. The Tariff Board's functions are threefold. First, they undertake inquiries into any issue relating to trade and commerce when asked by the Government. Second, the Tariff Board advises the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on tariff-related issues the Minister may refer to it such as the valuation of goods and the implications of adopting the harmonized system of tariff classification. Under a standing reference by the Minister of Finance, it inquires into complaints by Canadian industry as to whether imports at preferential tariffs granted to developing countries are causing injury.
Finally, the Tariff Board acts as an appeal tribunal primarily in customs and excise disputes. Most of the Tariff Board members' time is spent on the appeal function.
Canadian International Trade Tribunal
Madam Speaker, my colleague from Roberval (Mr. Bouchard) told me earlier this morning that he fully supports this Bill.
The main role of the Canadian Import Tribunal is to undertake material injury inquiries as part of anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations. I know that this is important to the riding of Roberval, Madam Speaker.
The Canadian Import Tribunal also undertakes general injury inquiries when requested by the Government.
Finally, Madam Speaker, the Textile and Clothing Board is primarily an advisory body. The Government can ask the board to give advice on any matter affecting the textile and clothing industry. Either the government or the textile and clothing industry can request the board to undertake an injury inquiry.
The TCB also monitors developments in the Canadian textile and clothing industry.
Madam Speaker, I would note that under the new Bill the Government will continue to be able to seek advice from the new tribunal on textile and clothing issues that may arise as it will be the case for any other sector. The government, through its relevant departments will continue to monitor development in that industry as it currently does for several other sectors.
Madam Speaker, this brief description highlights the degree of duplication and overlap that now exists and that a particular issue may be treated differently depending on the agency dealing with it.
If I may I will now turn to the powers and functions of the new tribunal which constitute the substantive provisions of the bill. The new Canadian International Trade Tribunal will take over the main functions of the three import institutions as well as being given an important new function. As such the Canadian International Trade Tribunal will be responsible for undertaking a wide variety of inquiries such as general economic inquiries, injury inquiries and tariff-related inquiries. In addition, it will take over responsibility for hearing appeals of customs and excise decisions that are currently heard by the Tariff Board.
Finally, the new tribunal will be given an important new inquiry function: hearing complaints by Canadian producers in any industry that increased imports are causing or threatening serious injury.
General Economic Inquiries. The legislation contains general inquiry provisions whereby the government can ask the tribunal to inquire into matters relating to the economic, commercial and trade interests of Canada. Such fact-finding inquiries could be made regarding goods or services. Their purpose is to give the Government an independent assessment as a basis for developing policies. Any Government reference to the tribunal under these provisions will specify the issues to be examined. An example of the kind of inquiry the new tribunal could be asked to undertake is the recent study by the Tariff Board regarding the economic prospects of the Canadi-ian natural sweetener industry.



April 21, 1988
Canadian International Trade Tribunal
Tariff-Related Inquiries. The tribunal will also undertake tariff-related inquiries when requested by the Minister of Finance. These inquiries are helpful in relation to the Minister's responsabilities for tariff policy.
A recent inquiry undertaken by the Tariff Board in this area was an analysis of the conversion of Canada's tariff to the harmonized commodity description and coding system. You will recall that legislation implementing the harmonized system was passed by this parliament late last year.
Another example of a tariff-related inquiry is the reference to the Tariff Board by the Minister of Finance to undertake inquiries at the request of Canadian producers as to whether general preferential tariff concessions unilateraly granted to developing countries are injurious to Canadian producers. The procedures associated with these inquiries are intended to be retained by the new tribunal.
Injury Inquiries. The new tribunal will have general responsibilities for all injury inquiries. However, the current "fast-track" procedures whereby producers of horticultural products can seek emergency safeguard action without reference to an independent tribunal will continue to be available. The most common of injury inquiries are those associated with anti-dumping and countervail cases initiated under the Special Import Measures Act. In addition, the Government will continue to be able to direct the tribunal to conduct general inquiries into the injurious impact of imports of goods or services. The specific authority to request such inquiries is now set out in the special import measures Act and, in the case of textile and clothing products, under the textile and clothing Board Act. Direct Access Injury Inquiries. The existing rights of the textile and clothing industry to directly petition an independent body for an injury inquiry will be extended to all industries. In such inquiries the tribunal will examine whether increased imports are a principal cause of serious injury to domestic producers of like goods. Until now, except for the textile and clothing industry, such inquiries could only be undertaken at the request of the government. It is important to note that the tribunal will only consider complaints under the direct access provisions where the cause of the alleged injury is increased imports of fairly traded goods. Complaints regarding injurious dumping or subsidization will continue to be dealt with under the anti-dumping or countervail provisions of the Special Import Measures Act.
The right of direct access is being extended to all producers to make the procedures of dealing with injury complaints by Canadian producers more equitable and open. The new system will be more transparent and clear for Canadian producers. There will no longer be any doubt in Canadian producer's
minds concerning the procedures to be followed when they feel that increased imports are causing them serious injury.
In extending the direct access to all industries the Government was mindful to ensure that frivolous, ill-founded, trade harassing complaints would not stand before the new tribunal. In this connection, it is worth recalling that the purpose of safeguard actions is to help an industry adjust to legitimate import competition. Such actions are therefore meant to be temporary and designed in such a way as to encourage such adjustment.
As you can see, Madam Speaker, there is widespread support for Bill C-110!
For a safeguard injury inquiry to be initiated by the new tribunal, certain conditions will therefore need to be met. For example, the petition must be made by firms producing the majority of the Canadian production of the goods to be investigated. Furthermore, producers will have to provide adequate evidence that increased imports are causing the alleged injury. These conditions should ensure that only legitimate complaints will be accepted by the tribunal.
The legislation contains provisions whereby the Government can ask the tribunal to investigate and report on related issues, at any time during or after a direct access inquiry. These issues could include such public interest matters as competition policy, competitiveness, prices and/or the availability of imports. They could also include the desirability of following various courses of action to deal with serious injury that may be caused by increased imports.
These provisions will allow the Government to have the public interest considered in the context of a direct access inquiry and when choosing to do so to tailor its intervention to the particularities of the case.
The decision regarding the taking of border action or any other appropriate measures pursuant to a serious injury report, resulting either from a government reference or a direct access petition, will continue to rest with the government. In making a decision on border action the Government will, among other things, take into account trade relations considerations, particularly since affected parties generally have rights under the GATT to compensation or to take equivalent action in retaliation when safeguard actions are taken.
Appeals. The new tribunal will take over the existing appeal function of the Tariff Board. This essentially involves the hearing of appeals of Revenue Canada decisions regarding customs and excise duties. The current attractive attributes of the Tariff Board process-ease of access, speediness, ability to represent self, informality, low costs-will be retained in the new tribunal. And I know, Madam speaker, that some people in the riding of Roberval have benefitted from this.
April 21, 1988

Madam Speaker, the other provisions of the bill deal essentially with the establishment of the new tribunal, organizational and procedural matters. Most of these provisions originate in the statutes of the existing tribunals, particularly the Canadian Import Tribunal which was established at the end of 1984.
The new tribunal will be composed of nine members appointed by Governor in Council. This is a significant reduction from the existing 15 members of the three agencies being replaced. This is made possible by the rationalization resulting from amalgamation. In order to deal with situations of heavy work-load, the law contains provisions for the appointment of temporary members. The chairman will be the Chief Executive Officer of the tribunal.
In developing this bill the government was concerned about maintaining the current "easy access" attributes of the existing institutions. The bill contains provisions which will ensure that this objective is met. For example, parties will continue to be able to appear in person before the tribunal and a provision specifically states that hearings must be conducted as informally as possible.
The bill contains several provisions which will ensure transparency. For example, public notice of reports and decisions of the new tribunal will be made. In the same vein, the bill provides for the making by the new tribunal of rules of procedures for the conduct of its proceedings and for the submission of an annual report on its activities as is currently the case for the Canadian Import Tribunal.
Finally, the bill contains detailed disclosure of information provisions which will ensure access by interested parties to information before the tribunal in the course of proceedings while at the same time protect information which must legitimately remain confidential.
Madam Speaker, I believe this bill will significantly modernize, rationalize and streamline Canadian import institutions. It puts an end to the duplication and overlap that now exists as well as to the confusion this may create. It will ensure that the government gets sound and consistent advice on trade-related matters. This is particularly important for a country like Canada where a major proportion of its wealth depends on trade. It will give to all Canadian producers an important new right to have their legitimate trade concerns heard by an independent tribunal. Since the Bill was first introduced in the House, we have not received any representations against the purpose of this Bill and I hope the House will give it speedy approval.

Madam Speaker, the Bill before us today, as the Parliamentary Secretary has said, creates a new agency, the Canadian International Trade Tribunal, by amalgamating three existing agencies, the Canadian Import Tribunal, the Tariff Board and the Textile and Clothing Board. The aim is to remove whatever duplication and overlap currently exists. Presumably, the new agency
Canadian International Trade Tribunal
will provide for greater harmonization and standardization in the way import issues are treated.
At present the Canadian Import Tribunal conducts inquiries into anti-dumping and countervail cases. It also has the responsibility for undertaking general injury inquiries when requested to do so by the Government.
The Tariff Board advises the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on matters of trade and economic issues and particularly tariff-related measures. It also acts as an appeal tribunal for disputes between importers and Revenue Canada regarding decisions made on excise tariff and other administrative matters. I will return to this appeal tribunal function later.
The Textile and Clothing Board, the third agency, gives advice on trade matters that affect the Canadian textile and clothing industries. The newest tribunal will be responsible for undertaking a wide variety of inquiries; general economic inquiries, injury inquiries and tariff-related inquiries. The Government will be able to ask the tribunal to inquire into matters relating to the trade interests of Canada under the rubric of the general economic inquiries. Examples of injury inquiries are anti-dumping and countervail cases. However, the current fast-track procedures whereby producers of horticultural products can seek emergency safeguard action without reference to an independent tribunal will continue to be available.
The direct access injury inquiries, such as the existing rights of the textile and clothing industry to petition directly the Textile and Clothing Board for an injury inquiry, will be extended to all industries. At present only the Government can initiate such an inquiry for other industries. In the case of the tariff-related inquiries, the tribunal would conduct these when requested to do so by the Minister of Finance. Therefore, the Government is still maintaining a fair amount of control over the access to this independent tribunal.
The new tribunal takes over the appeal function of the Tariff Board involving appeals of Revenue Canada decisions regarding customs and excise duties. The new tribunal will be composed of nine instead of the present fifteen members. Therefore, essentially, the present members will be competing for their jobs since the tribunal is not yet established.
We may very well find ourselves faced with a similar situation as that of the Immigration Appeal Board. Recently the Federal Court of Canada ruled that the Government's refugee Bill, Bill C-55, created "a reasonable apprehension of bias" on the part of the Immigration Appeal Board because the Government proposes to fire all its members and rehire only some of them. Therefore, according to the court, the board could appear to lean in favour of the Government's position in immigration cases where the situation arose where the board members were in effect competing for their jobs. That specific ruling, which was rendered in March, was that the present Immigration Appeal Board was prohibited from determining the refugee status of one applicant "for as long as a reasonable apprehension of bias exists", and immigration lawyers have said that that ruling affects every refugee claimant in Canada.

April 21, 1988
Canadian International Trade Tribunal
If the same principle is applied to this Bill before us, if someone chooses to challenge that, we may find that the situation of fifteen members of the three amalgamated tribunals competing for nine jobs may create "a reasonable apprehension of bias" that toward the Government's position and industry may find itself without the access to appeals which the Bill promises until the matter is cleared up by the courts.
I also want to speak particularly about the apparel trade. In Canada, unlike the United States, we find a certain rift, or at least there are different interests presented by the Apparel Manufacturers Institute and the textile trade. In the United States the two work together and form a very effective and, unfortunately, very protectionist lobby. Recently, the Minister of Finance told members of the Canadian Apparel Manufacturers Institute that the Government was determined to give clothing manufacturers a fighting chance to compete in their own market against the Americans, and that the high tariffs on foreign textiles, which run on average about twice as high as comparable U.S. external tariffs, would be reduced to at least U.S. levels over the the 1990s.
This will not guarantee survival under free trade for Canadian apparel manufacturers but it will help lower their input costs since they now import about 60 per cent of their fabrics from third countries. I am not talking about low cost, low quality goods, but rather about many of the high quality fabrics and textiles which are used for Canada's most stylish clothing products. However, the trouble is that most of the tariff relief is in the future and will be shaped by this new government regulatory body, the Canadian International Trade Tribunal, which may very well find itself limited in what it can do. Although the tribunal is theoretically independent, it will of course hear not only from manufacturers but from the textile makers, who have a totally different set of priorities and interests and whose lobbying was responsible for the erecting of these high tariff walls, in the first place.
Some time ago the Government announced and began to shape a massive duty remission package which would have cost $2 billion in lost revenues over 10 years. This was designed to assist the apparel manufacturers. However, when word of the package reached the United States and its powerful protectionist textile industry, the reaction was fierce and fast.
The Minister backed off and the duty remission portion of the policy was scaled down, with the major part of the tariff relief policy being pushed into the future and extended to cover both textile and apparel industries. To make it additionally palatable, Canada gave the U.S. a partial or total preference on several immediate tariff reductions for specialty fabrics or yarns not made in Canada.
This will present the Canadian apparel manufacturers with a number of difficulties both because of the preference and also because of the rules of origin. Canadian manufacturers will be driven to find American rather than third country
sources of fabrics wherever possible in order to qualify for duty-free access to the United States market beyond a stipulated quota.
The North American market is very difficult. Some Canadian clothing manufacturers will survive. They will perhaps find themselves specialty niches such as winter clothing. Some may be able to maintain their markets because of being so near, if they are able to provide very quick and effective supply. However, increasingly, the industry will be facing a great deal of restructuring.
Canadian manufacturers are saying that it is no longer enough to manufacture a few good items of clothing, that the industry trend is to product lines manufactured, assembled and marketed to retail chains. That takes size and export and marketing skills. There is really no guarantee of success even in the domestic market after putting out all these additional moneys.
Thus Canadian suppliers are facing a difficult time. It will not be a smooth restructuring. The situation is complicated because the industry is divided. The situation in the United States, where textiles and clothing manufacturers work together as a very large and very effective lobby, leaves our Canadian manufacturers and our Canadian textile industry much more vulnerable. I am not sure that the creation of this additional international trade tribunal, which simply delays the process of finding solutions, is the way to go at this particular time.
There is one significant exclusion upon which I wish to comment before giving the floor to some of the other Members who I know wish to speak on this matter. It is that the international import tribunal is not empowered to inquire into or otherwise administer complaints that involve dumping or subsidization of imported goods. Such questions in the future are to be referred to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) to be dealt with under the Special Import Measures Act.
That does not inspire confidence, not with a Government like this, which has shown such a singular lack of backbone in standing up to American pressures. We have to be very uneasy with the present Government about any move that increases ministerial discretion and takes matters of trade dispute away from an independent tribunal with public hearings where Canadians can be fully informed.

Madam Speaker, first I would like to suggest that this is a Bill which is actually more controversial than the Government suggested in its opening comments. Certainly, in our discussions with a number of groups throughout the country, in particular groups which were previously subject to the Textile and Clothing Board, which had certain powers and certain capacities to act which this particular new international trade tribunal will not have, they have expressed to us their serious concerns about what the Government is doing in this case.
April 21, 1988

I must say that we have also had from a number of importers and import competing institutions a sense that this Bill is really far too weak when compared to what they had hoped to see come forward from the Government, given the much more difficult international situation which our traders face throughout the world. Frankly, it is for that reason that it is somewhat disappointing that the Minister is not here to carry forward this debate today.
I must also make the point that there are a great many parts of the Bill which we find to be half-hearted, timid, timorous and which give one a sense of taking steps backward at a time when we should be taking steps forward to try to establish a more dynamic institution which could act more effectively on behalf of Canadian businesses and Canadian workers.
Despite these basic concerns which we intend to raise in the form of amendments at the legislative committee stage we still as a Party support the basic principle of the Bill. That principle is to streamline, rationalize and obtain a more effective single institution which can serve the important needs of Canadian business at the present time with the great escalation of what has to be considered unfair competition internationally. The situation must certainly be considered much more competitive and threatening to exports from this country than has been true in the past, exports to other markets which we have considered to rest with us in the past.
This sense of trying to pull together the three institutions which have dealt with trade policy restrictions in the past is something which we think makes sense. The reduction of a number of agencies operating in this field, we also think is important. It seems to us that it is not sensible to have three separate bodies dealing very much with the same type of concerns in relation to trade, all of them building up sources of expertise and manpower to support them. That type of proliferation of government agencies seems to us both unnecessary and wasteful, as far as the public is concerned.
But if we are aiming to pull together these three institutions into one effective and dynamic institution, I believe it is necessary that we do it very differently from what this Bill has set out to do with respect to a number of the key details of the Bill itself. Some of those details will be debated at much greater length in the legislative committee. But I do not think that the Government should simply assume that it has an uncontroversial Bill before the House which will simply sail through without a lot of questions being raised by the opposition Parties. These questions have certainly been raised with us by the people who will be affected by this change in institutions.
There is a certain irony that while we are taking backward steps with respect to what some of our institutions have been
Canadian International Trade Tribunal
able to do, especially the Textile and Clothing Board, this very day the United States is voting on an omnibus Trade Bill which will not reduce the powers of its International Trade Commission, but, rather, will increase them very considerably. It will also increase the powers of the United States trade representative very considerably. It will provide a greater arm's length relationship between the Government and the various institutions regulating international trade in the United States.
In short, if the omnibus Trade Bill passes today, as everybody predicts, the United States will be setting up a system which will establish weapons which it has developed for the increasingly tough international trade wars that are taking place which are very much more powerful, quicker in their capacity to respond, and more independent and therefore responsive to business' and workers' concerns within the United States.
While the United States is doing that, we have before us a Bill which, in a number of very important respects, weakens the capacity of Canadian business and the capacity of Canadian workers to take the tough steps that are often needed to deal with unfair trade activities occurring within the international economy.
If I may point out some of those concerns in particular, they start with the speed with which this tribunal will be able to move. In Canada, that has certainly been a problem in the past. For instance, it is not uncommon for the Tariff Board to take a year to hear appeals on tariff classifications or valuation issues which come before the Tariff Board. In fact, the average length of time taken is one year. That is clearly not fast enough to respond to the concerns of Canadians workers and business people who want to get a decision from the Tariff Board.
I have great deal of concern looking at this so-called rationalization that by reducing the number of people who will be involved in this process, potentially we will make it an even lengthier and more difficult process for Canadian workers and business people to get decisions from this institution. Therefore, speed is the first concern. Is this in fact an effective institution that will be created that will be able to respond rapidly to problems of unfair trade, as is often crucial in the international economy these days? I have a serious doubt in my mind with respect to the question of speed.
Second, the Textile and Clothing Board, the TCB, has had within its powers one important function, and that has been the independent capacity to initiate inquiries with respect to dangers to the industry, with respect to questions of adjustment and restructuring within the industry, and with respect to questions which involve the future of workers within that industry.

April 21, 1988
Canadian International Trade Tribunal
That is not a power that has been associated with the International Trade Tribunal. It is not a power that has been associated the Tariff Board. However, in attempting to put these three bodies together, the sensible thing to do would surely be to recognize that the power which existed with the TCB has been a useful, effective and responsive power which has made it possible for the Textile and Clothing Board to move quickly to initiate inquiries when it was crucial. In attempting to rationalize all three of these institutions, surely the sensible and efficient thing to do would be to give the producers the capacity to look for assistance when unfair trading is taking place. Surely the sensible thing to do would be to give to this new tribunal the power which the Textile and Clothing Board had. However, that is not what has been done.
Instead, the power which existed with the TCB has been stripped away. The new tribunal will not have the power to take independent initiatives on problems which may occur in the future. That seems to me to be a serious mistake and a question with which we will attempt to deal in committee.
Third, besides conducting inquiries, it has been possible in the past for a board such as the Textile and Clothing Board to actually make recommendations to the Government. If the board discovers, for instance, that there is import action which is seriously hurting a sector of the Canadian industry, it has been possible for the TCB to recommend to the Government specifically what it feels should be done. That has been a key part of this institution's activities. Yet this Bill strips that power away from the TCB. The Bill sets up a tribunal which itself is much less powerful, precisely because it cannot do what its equivalent in the United States will be able to do, which is to make direct recommendations about what should be done to counter an import threat of some kind which is hurting Canadian producers.
Again, I have a sense of irony, almost a sense of unreality, about the Government's weakness as it sets up a new institution here in Canada after looking at the one in the United States. The International Trade Commission in the United States has complete authority to make recommendations. No one there would think of establishing an institution which did not have that authority, and in fact, the omnibus Trade Bill which is being voted on today increases the capacity of the United States ITC to make such recommendations in the future. That increases the necessity of institutions elsewhere in the United States trade mix to respond to those recommendations from the ITC. Yet here in Canada, we are taking a backward step by providing that in the future, the International Trade Tribunal will not have the capacity to make recommendations to the Government with respect to any trade problem it has discovered.
It is not simply weak of the Government to be doing this, it is also stupid. The Government is creating a collection of expertise, and that expertise should surely be employed not just to assess import problems or trade threats but also to make recommendations, based on that expertise, as to how the Government should respond to that difficulty.
Fourth, I must deal with the question of direct access. Almost three years ago now, a special committee was established to look at international relations, a joint Senate and House committee. That committee recommended that we should have a much stronger and more flexible single international trade tribunal and that it should be possible for Canadian businesses to access that trade tribunal directly.
In this Bill, the Government pretends that it has established that direct access. In fact, however, the details of the Bill show that the principle of direct access is trumpeted but the reality of direct access is prevented. Let me point out two specific ways in which this is true.
First, it is not possible for companies to have direct access with respect to countervail actions. Countervail actions have become the heart of the international trade conflict which is taking place in the world today. Yet this Bill suggests that companies will not have direct access with respect to this absolutely crucial part of trading activities and policies. They will have direct access to everything else, but they will not have direct access to what really counts. Surely that too is a weak and foolish step to take.
I must also say that it is a very curious principle that this direct access to the new institution will only be possible if companies from an industry can prove that they are speaking on behalf of a majority of that industry. What does that mean? For example, textile companies based in the Atlantic provinces feel they are being attacked by unfair trade practices on the part of another country. It is not possible for them to take their case to this new import tribunal. The case has to be taken there by a majority of the industry across the country. It might be that the industry in Quebec and Ontario, which would make up the majority, would be quite pleased to see their competitors in Atlantic Canada go down the drain and would not support their Atlantic counterparts in taking their case to the tribunal. That would stop the Atlantic producers from having an inquiry take place.
Exactly the same is true of western producers of, let us say, steel. For example, both Saskatchewan and British Columbia produce small but important amounts of steel. They might want to take a case to this new tribunal saying that they are being damaged by imports. Yet they are not permitted to do so because the rest of the industry concentrated in central Canada refuses to go along with their concern. This could be because the industry in central Canada wishes to see the industry in western Canada wiped out as a future competitor.
Again, this seems to me to be a ridiculous, weak and misguided attempt to set the parameters for this institution. In short, we are likely to find ourselves in a situation where it is not possible for certain parts of the country affected by import pressure to take their case to this tribunal unless they have a majority of the entire industry across the country with them. Even if they do that, they cannot do it with respect to unfair trade in the way of countervailing duties.
April 21, 1988

There is a fifth point, the last key weakness in this Bill. If we want to put together a body of serious expertise able to operate effectively in this tough international environment, why do we not give that institution much more freedom than is established by this Bill? As I have noted, it is not possible for countervailing duty issues to be considered by the tribunal unless there is a reference from the Governor in Council, in fact the whole Cabinet. Why do we want to control this institution so closely? What is it about the Textile and Clothing Board which has been so ineffective in the past? In fact, that board, with its sense of greater freedom, has been able to be quite effective and efficient with respect to many of the inquiries it has initiated and its analysis of issues with respect to countervailing duties. Yet the Government is preventing this new institution, which it says is supposed to be more effective and efficient, from operating on its own. I just do not understand the logic. It seems it can only be justified by a sense of wanting to create some kind of institution dealing with trade without actually establishing a serious and substantive institution.
It is for that reason that the fight which will take place in committee to try to establish a serious international trade tribunal will be extremely long and hard. It will be necessary to call as many witnesses as we need to convince the Government that it is establishing a hollow shell instead of a tough and efficient institution which can act on behalf of Canadian producers in the future. That is what the Government has brought on itself by not consulting with as wide a sector of the industry as it should have. It did not consult with workers and their institutions. It certainly did not consult with the opposition Parties. It is certainly not attempting to open up to broader public discussion the question of what kind of institution we need. That is a recipe for serious problems in getting the Bill through the Elouse in the short time available before the summer recess and a possible election.
Frankly, I am quite sad that the Government chose this approach. It has taken a good and sensible idea and put it together in such a way as to vitiate the idea. It has weakened it and, as I said, created the form but not the substance of what producers in the international economy will need in the very difficult days in the future.

Madam Speaker, last night I was driven to amusement by the appearance of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on national television protesting his innocence on matters of patronage. I knew that pending on the legislative timetable was Bill C-110, one of the most blatant and egregious examples of the Government's horrendous appetite for finding places for its favourite colleagues. More important, this Bill has created a serious level of confusion in the procedures of trade remedy law in the country.
On March 15 the case of Maltby versus the Minister of National Revenue before the Tariff Board was referred to the Federal Court because of the clear apprehension of bias which was created as a result of the Bill which we are debating at
Canadian International Trade Tribunal
second reading today. This Bill contains clauses which permit the extermination of the existing members of all tariff boards and agencies in Canada without any form of severance or allowance for services.
The precedent was set with the Immigration Appeal Board when the Government undertook the ridiculous initiative of firing all the people on the board without any of the due processes which are generally allowed for under our Labour Code. The incredible confusion in the immigration system has now been compounded by the fact that the Immigration Appeal Board cannot work. We now have a similar circumstance with the tariff boards.
The Prime Minister of Canada is saying, "My hands are clean, my conscience is clear, we do things totally in the public interest without any advantage being sought". Yet, we have two Bills still before Parliament, one on immigration and one on tariffs, in which the Government is executing the most severe and blatant example of trying to eliminate people in quasi-judicial positions whose independence is absolutely sacrosanct, thereby creating a clear apprehension of bias to the point where the courts of the country have now endorsed that position. The Federal Court has always said, in the case of the Immigration Appeal Board, that there is an apprehension of bias, and that particular regulatory agency has now ground to a halt.
I think it would be very important, perhaps for the Clerks or the Speaker's office, to determine whether this legislation in fact contravenes some of the basic rules. If you are creating that apprehension and bias you are running into clear legal jurisdictional problems. This certainly gives full lie to the speech made by the Prime Minister yesterday and will be one of the clear exhibits which the people of Canada will have in front of them of the appetite the Government has shown. It is not satisfied simply to replace people as their terms come to an end, but most commit a form of guillotine on sitting Members in order to get their own partisans on these boards and agencies. The Government is thereby clearly guilty of interfering in the quasi-judicial regulatory structure of the country.
I do not think that any other Government in the history of this country has ever undertaken that kind of action. That is why this Bill, with some laudable purposes in terms of trying to reform the trade mechanism, because of that voracious appetite for patronage has turned into a very ugly piece of legislation which has very serious overtones which go beyond simply matters of trade.
That is why we find this piece of legislation as repugnant as we did Bill C-55, which was repugnant for a number of reasons dealing with human rights and individual liberties. However, the fact that this Bill has built into it a clear and unmistakable whiff of patronage of the most evident and manifest kind will result in other Canadians finding it equally repugnant. That is unfortunate because reform is required in our trade administration. There must be better rationalization for determining trade remedy laws.

April 21, 1988
Canadian International Trade Tribunal
I do not understand why the Government does things like this. I do not understand why it takes something which could have been useful, could have been purposeful, could have been positive, and perverts it so badly. It was unnecessary. There is attrition. People resign their offices. They do not have to be kicked out summarily by a piece of legislation, thereby destroying the whole system. That was not necessary. It is not contingent to the effective utilization of this Bill. The Government is blinded by the thought that it may not be here much longer and wants to get its friends into cushy jobs for the next 10 years. This kind of philosophy has biased a good piece of legislation. As I said, it is just not necessary to do those kinds of things and establish such a precedent.
I fully expect that the Federal Court will rule on this legislation in the same way as it did on Bill C-55. I expect that it will rule that it is the cause of a clear apprehension of bias in the present operations of our regulatory system. Therefore, all the cases presently before the import tribunals will not be able to be considered until we expunge this particular set of clauses from the Bill. Members opposite should be duly warned that that is going to have to happen, that they cannot contravene basic principles of regulatory law, which is what they are doing with this legislation. It will be our responsibility to ensure that we cleanse it of this particular obvious and evident maladministration of our trade law.
Speaking of that. Madam Speaker, my Party has put forward a number of proposals over the last two years on how we should rationalize and reorganize the trade administration system in Canada in keeping with the new international trade atmosphere which we face. As a piece of legislation this is simply tinkering, it is not doing what we would have liked, that is, rewriting the trade law itself to ensure that Canadian producers facing competition, facing the requirement to offset unfair trade practices of other countries, will be able to receive fair and adequate protection. We can say quite honestly that our trade law is not adequate for the task, nor is our trade machinery.
Let me give one very clear example of where a serious omission has been made, and that is in the area of adjustment. We have done an awful lot of experimentation in the last 10 years to try to find ways to assist industry in dealing with the dislocations that are caused by international competition, by trade competition. As tariffs have come down as a consequence of various GATT rounds, we have attempted, through such things as the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board to help industry meet that kind of competition. The Canadian Industrial Renewal Board was a separate agency administered by a board composed of people from the private sector. It was meant to provide both labour adjustment and capital adjustment to the footwear and textile industries to help them meet that kind of competition and allow them to modernize.
Similarly, our administration brought in the Industrial Labour Adjustment Program which was designed to help
individual industries like the automobile sector which was facing a downturn in 1980, or the textile and other sectors to provide assistance to workers for retraining or pre-retirement benefits, as well as to give industrial assistance to firms or communities.
Those programs were wiped out by the Government. In some cases, it allowed them to lapse, such as with the retirement benefits for older workers. The Canadian Industrial Renewal Board was allowed to lapse, but nothing was put in its place.
I am not saying that those instruments were perfect. They were experiments in recognition that something had to be done to deal with the major problem of industrial adjustment in this country. However, if it was the judgment of the Government in 1984 that these programs were not good enough, it should have introduced something better. Instead, it created a vacuum, and there is no adequate means of enabling industries to respond to dislocation, to help workers affected by competition or to give some security for our workforce in light of the new trade conditions.
Approximately one month ago, the Economic Council published a report entitled "Managing Adjustment: Policies for Trade Sensitive Industries". The Council made a very clear set of recommendations that the new Canadian import tribunal should have the ability to provide for adjustments or forms of protection for industries affected by international competition. The Economic Council indicated that in order to make it work effectively a broad-based set of instruments had to be available. I do not believe anyone on the government side is suspicious of the Economic Council, which tends to endorse all of the Government's initiatives.
The question is why the Government did not respond at least to these set of recommendations and say that one of the powers of the new tribunal would be to ensure that the tribunal would be able to make a judgment, whether it be in the form of temporary quotas or direct assistance to the workers in the particular industry. Part of its responsibility should be to make such a judgment, for example, in the case of a town affected by the closure of its textile plant because of a new high technology area or a trade arrangement. In my opinion, Bill C-l 10 contains no such powers.
For example, the Employment Support Act, passed in 1972, is still on the statute books of Canada. It was brought in by a previous Liberal administration when the United States introduced its 10 per cent surtax under the Nixon administration. That Employment Support Act enabled Canadian industry to stay in business while we reconciled that particular conflict. Those industries did not have to shut down because they were able to get assistance to fight those particular incursions. As a result, some 5,000 Canadian businesses kept their doors open during that period.
April 21, 1988

The Employment Support Act has been put in abeyance. It could be brought off the shelf and reactivated with the new Canadian International Trade Tribunal as the agency to make the judgment as to when and how support for workers could be provided as a result of international trade competition.
The Government is contemplating signing an agreement with the United States which will require massive adjustments in this country. The Bank of Nova Scotia, an agency to which I presume the Government would listen, has listed some 17 to 20 different industries that will face massive relocation. The only response we have received so far from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and others is that they will use existing programs to provide that adjustment. However, existing programs have been cut back by 30 per cent. The labour adjustment and training programs have been cut back by 30 percent. How will it be possible to deal with this new adjustment when the funds are being severely cut? It does not make sense. Furthermore, the existing programs are not trade sensitive.
We are still waiting with great anticipation for some kind of older worker adjustment program, the people affected most directly when an industry must shut down or change its technology as a consequence of trade or other matters.
The promise was made over a year ago and we are near the end of the legislative agenda, but nothing has happened. Simple amendments to this legislation would enable us to provide for labour adjustment for older workers affected by trade dislocation. I believe it is a prime opportunity for the Government to fulfil a promise that it made over a year ago because it could easily be done in this legislation.
The Economic Council study described in principle how it could be implemented. The fact that this legislation has those omissions only indicates to me that the Government has no intention of bringing in adjustment programs. It made a false promise to older workers and has no interest in providing any kind of federal government support.
This does not mean there will be no adjustment assistance, it will simply have to be picked up by the provinces or the private sector, adding costs to their budgets which have not been in any way provided for. The Minister of Finance may be able to keep his own financial books in order, but when we look at the national accounts of Canada we see that someone will have to pay for thousands of workers who will be affected.
It will certainly be our intention in dealing with this legislation to make the tribunal a far more contemporary instrument of dealing with trade sensitive adjustment programs than anything that is presently provided for by the Government. If the Government will not do it, someone will have to, and I only hope that members of the government caucus would be aware of their obligation in this respect and support those kinds of amendments that will have to be introduced.
Canadian International Trade Tribunal
Finally, let me point out that I also believe the trade law itself needs to be reformed. The reorganization of the tribunal is not good enough. The tribunal is only as good as the law it must implement and, as we have seen in the recent Hyundai case, our present anti-dumping rules are not sufficient to encompass the kind of new conditions we face whereby corporations are making different products in different countries with a market system that requires a different test for countervail or dumping. Again, it would seem to me that a corollary piece of legislation, if not included in this, must be a very major overhaul in rewriting of our trade law generally to catch up with modern contemporary circumstances.
Those are only some of the reasons that I think this is a deeply flawed piece of legislation. The Government has taken what should have been a good idea and failed very badly in its execution both because of what it omits and because of the very severe perversion of the Act in terms of trying to exterminate existing members of the tribunals we now have in a way that can only be interpreted as an appetite for the patronage machine of the Conservative Party.

Madam Speaker, I have just one question that I would like to raise with my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). I would like to refer specifically to the Textile and Clothing Board and the particular powers it has had in the past, powers which have given the board the capacity to initiate inquiries of its own which, in turn, gave the board the possibility, indeed, the duty, of making recommendations to go with its findings from inquiries.
I know the Member is a fellow member of several committees looking at trade matters, and of course a fellow member of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade. I would be interested in his explanation or analysis of why he feels the Government, in amalgamating the three institutions, has cut out those key functions which the Textile and Clothing Board in the past was quite successfully able to fulfil. What explanation would the Hon. Member offer of that, to me, very strange and very foolish move?

Madam Speaker, I did not address that specific part of the legislation, first, because I thought the Hon. Member himself had dealt with it so adequately and, second, because time was a constraint. However, I would want to offer my own sense of puzzlement as to why what was a useful and effective power is being stripped. I can only suggest two things; first, there is an increasing tendency on the part of the Government to strip down the arm's length relationship between itself and a number of agencies, to politicize, in effect, the kind of quasi-judicial system which has been used in this country for a long time.

April 21, 1988
Canadian International Trade Tribunal
As the Hon. Member knows, I spoke on the one area where it is stripping the members out, and I think it is again an attempt to try to control decisions, especially because of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. I think the Government recognizes there are going to be a number of new areas of sensitivity growing up. It does not want someone else out there examining them in an independent way and reaching conclusions the Government may not like. I think it is quite a deliberate attempt to squelch and restrict the orbit of independent inquiry, examination or initiative because of the potential embarrassment of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. I really believe that is reason number one.
Second, I also believe we are again seeing a tendency, one that disturbs me, to have our trade matters basically decided in the Department of External Affairs itself. I think my own Government takes some responsibility for this when it amalgamated the Department of Trade, the Department of External Affairs and others and made trade a kind of handmaiden to foreign policy, as opposed to trade as a direct outcome of domestic needs and the requirement of our own producers to go out and get markets. I think we have reversed the onus as to what our trade policy should be. As a result, we do not want these agencies doing things the Department of External Affairs does not want them to do. It is just part and parcel of the same area. Again, it may result in different sensitivities. We know there is an incredibly difficult balancing act going on in the textile area between the importation of low-cost products from Third World countries and the protection of our own domestic industry. I think that is an area that we as a country must come to grips with in a more effective way than we have.
Unfortunately, the way in which it could have been done more effectively, through the Textile and Clothing Board, will no longer be allowed. It will now be in the hands of a Minister to determine whether and how they are going to do it. So I think that restriction on those freedoms is really a consequence of a kind of political and bureaucratic agenda on how to deal with trade policy.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate today on Bill C-110, an Act to establish the Canadian International Trade Tribunal. We have heard some interesting and useful remarks this morning, as is often the case, only from the opposition Parties. It seems to me that even with the largest majority in Canadian history, government Members cannot seem to pull themselves together to speak on any legislation.
There are some fundamental questions one has to ask oneself when looking at a Bill such as this Act to establish the Canadian International Trade Tribunal and to amend or repeal other Acts in consequence thereof. I think we have to ask ourselves if it does cut red tape. How accessible will it be to those who would want to use it? Is it at arm's length? Is it likely to be independent? And does it have real power?
The question of the arm's length relationship is perhaps one on which we should focus first. The new tribunal will not have the power to initiate inquiries, nor can it make recommendations for remedial action. I think that is a fundamental test
that any piece of legislation should be put to. Is it going to be at arm's length and can it do what the Government is trying to sell it as being able to do?
We can look under the clauses related to powers, duties and functions and find quite quickly that this has been designed in a certain way by the Government and by those who drafted this Bill. Clause 16 states that the duties and functions of the tribunal are to conduct inquiries, consider complaints, to hear, determine and deal with all appeals and exercise and perform such other duties or functions. One quickly sees that the Governor in Council, the Cabinet and the Minister have maintained control over the processes which might be launched under the new tribunal thoroughly and totally.
I think the points made by my friends, the Hon. Member for Essex Windsor (Mr. Langdon) and the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), make clear the question: if we are going to have a body, if we are going to amalgamate a number of other tribunals, reduce the number of members of that tribunal, obviously increase the work-load of a smaller number of individuals, are we actually providing powers? Are we actually making it independent so that a producer from wherever in Canada, whether from British Columbia, Prince Edward Island or Yellowknife, actually has access to a tribunal that is truly independent and can look at the real ramifications and causes of the complaint?
If we look at the first section under inquiries, inquiries into economic trade or commercial matters, we see it is strictly for the Governor in Council, so it is a political matter the Minister might bring to Cabinet, saying: "Here is something we should inquire into". Inquiries into tariff-related matters and inquiries into injuries are all very well laid out in terms of reference, tabling of reports, and so on. That is the political area. If there is some political heat coming from a collection of producers or from a number of regions or a number of provinces, the Minister in Cabinet can make a decision to send it on to the tribunal.
When we come to the clause on complaints by domestic producers, there is certainly a great deal of verbiage. There is Clause 22, Clause 23, and on and on it goes for pages about what a domestic producer would have to go through. There are 21-day time limits, 30-day time limits, reporting periods of 180 days and so on. When one moves on to Clauses 25, 26 and so on, one sees that they all lead once again right back to the Minister and the Cabinet.
A domestic producer might say, "Is that a little unusual in a piece of legislation?" It certainly is, if the Government is trying to sell this as cutting red tape, getting rid of three boards and making it one. It sounds great. It sounds like streamlining, government efficiency and cutting down on government debt, wastage and bureaucrats and so on. However, I have not even heard members of the Government trying to sell it as that.


April 21, 1988

When one looks at what type of real access domestic producers would have, one finds that it is likely to be stifled and snuffed out if any political waves might be made. Members who have already spoken have pointed out that in sensitive areas of obvious deficiency such as in the Mulroney-Reagan deal, areas in which our domestic producers will likely be harmed by certain things that will now be allowed under that agreement, should it be promulgated, they will not have the type of opportunity to be heard by an independent process. This is something that is fundamentally important and is provided by many other legislatures and parliaments around the world. In this way there is a truly independent arm's length operation.
All of the drafting of the Bill leads it back into the situation wherein it can be manipulated politically either by the Minister or by the Cabinet. In some cases it can be diverted off to the Deputy Minister of National Revenue for consideration under another Act, the Special Import Measures Act.
On the test of its independence it fails. On the test of its relevance, its accessibility and its timeliness for domestic producers, it fails, and it fails miserably.
I was always interested in listening to Conservative Members in opposition berate the Liberals when I was elected here in my second term in 1980 to 1984. They berated Liberals for bringing forward legislation without the accompanying regulations. They were always saying, "We are always expected to buy a pig in a poke". Now that the Conservatives are in government, they are even worse than the Liberals were in continually promulgating legislation before the House. The Government has been in office for four years. Surely, the regulations associated with this particular Bill could have been provided to Members of the House so that we could make a realistic evaluation of the legislation.
Let us look at Clause 40 of the Bill, which is now becoming standard Tory fare. They print a few pages with a few general themes but they never put the regulations in place. For example, even on definitions with respect to what is a domestic producer the Governor in Council has yet to make a regulation. This clause is worth reading into the record because it reveals that the Conservatives are once again bringing in a true pig in the poke before the House and asking it to be passed in its entirety. It states:
The Governor in Council may make regulations.
(a)	respecting the matters to be addressed or examined by the Tribunal in an inquiry-
That means that we do not even know what matters may be addressed or examined by the tribunal. We have a general idea. It will be almost impossible for a domestic producer to get anywhere unless the Minister is on side and the Cabinet is on side. If there are any political problems associated with having evidence heard before the tribunal then it will be
Canadian International Trade Tribunal
squashed by the Minister or by Cabinet before the producer even has a hearing. We now find that the definitions are not even provided to us. We read:
(b)	defining the expressions "domestic producer", "domestic production" and "like or directly competitive goods" for the purposes of this Act-
Those definitions are yet to be made by the Governor in Council. They will be promulgated after the Act is dealt with by Parliament. Once again, this is a truly undemocratic way of dealing with legislation. It reads:
(c)	defining the expression "other interested party" for the purposes of section 25, 26, 28, 29 or 30-
This is where domestic producers are in the midst of their process of identifying the problem that they have and trying to get themselves before the tribunal. We find that even in terms of defining other interested parties it has not been defined. For example, let us say that there is a domestic producer of a commodity in British Columbia who feels that there are other interested parties, perhaps someone who produces part of that commodity from, say, Calgary, Regina, Montreal or St. John's, Newfoundland, and wants to bring them in as an interested party because of the impact that certain imports might have on them. That is not being made available to them. I see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) nodding in agreement. Once again, we have a pig in a poke before the House.
One could drive a Kenworth truck through Clause 40 as a result of this type of loophole. It reads:
(d)	prescribing any matter or thing that under this Act may or is to be prescribed-
The real coup de grace of the Bill, a test that any Member of Parliament must put a piece of legislation to, is the following which states:
(e)	generally, for carrying out the purposes and provisions of this Act.
There is the big Kenworth. It allows the Government to turn this Bill, this paper tiger as it is presently written, into anything the Government should so desire.
Let us take a look at what the Government claims Bill C-110 does. It claims that it amalgamates three existing agencies: the Canadian Import Tribunal, known as CIT; the Tariff Board, known as TB; and the Textile and Clothing Board, the TCB. There is no doubt that it does that. It wipes out their legislative foundation and will turn them all into the Canadian International Trade Tribunal.
The duties and functions of the new tribunal are to inquire and report on economic trade or commercial matters as requested by the Government. Let us make sure that everyone in the country understands. This is not an independent tribunal where domestic producers, friends of the Minister of Transport, might have an opportunity to come to have a hearing before the board.

April 21, 1988
You are not very convincing.

The Minister of Transport says that I am very convincing. I am sure he will go back to Cabinet and make sure that this Bill is rewritten.
The Bill is to require a report to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and, as I referred to earlier, to refer some matters to National Revenue, including Canada's international rights and obligations. The terms and reference for both are then set by the Government.
In addition to its research functions, and this is where there is a problem, the tribunal cannot independently initiate its own inquiries into matters. They can only really come from the Minister or Cabinet. It is true that domestic producers can try to wind their way through, but before they ever actually complete the process it has to have the stamp of approval of the Minister or Cabinet. So how likely is it that that will happen in the case of a sensitive trade matter when we find out that the Minister for International Trade and Mr. Reisman bungled? Let us say that they forgot something and there is a little area there. The Government can say that this is embarrassing and that people will know there are a great many termite holes in this agreement. It will keep it to the side, whether it is a horticultural matter, a domestically produced commodity or whatever.
That reminds me, back in 1975 the then Liberal Government lifted the tariff and non-tariff barriers on Canadian household appliances. I refer to pop-up toasters, fridges, stoves, dishwashers and all that kind of thing. At that time we produced 90 per cent of our home appliances. They were purchased in Canada and made in Canada in Vancouver, Edmonton and various other centres across the country such as Toronto, Montreal and so on. After 10 years of having that tariff and non-tariff barrier removed, which was about a 4 per cent barrier to incoming products, there has been a complete reversal. Some 90 per cent of home appliances purchased in Canada are made in the United States.
We must ask ourselves this. Would this legislation meet the test of Canadian home appliance producers if we found ourselves in the situation of 1975 today in terms of that level of production? Would they be able to wind their way through, if they were having unfair dumping and unfair practices from another country, the United States or anywhere else? Would this type of tribunal provide timely, easily accessible and independent hearings and inquiries? The answer is no. I say that because it has been clutched so tightly politically to the body politic in this case to the Conservative Government, that it fails on all those really key tests. It is unlikely to be either accessible or useful to domestic producers.
I see that it is one o'clock. I will resume my comments later in the day.

subsubtopic: SITUATION OF PERSONS LIVING BELOW POVERTY LINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in spite of the economic recovery in our country, Statistics Canada confirms that the percentage of Canadians living below the poverty line has increased.
These statistics are upsetting and support our statements to the effect that only couples where both spouses work outside the home have been able to maintain their standard of living, compared to couples living on one salary, who have seen their income drop by 4 per cent.
The situation of young couples has deteriorated to such an extent that their children-our children, Mr. Speaker-are living in poverty. One out of five children in Canada is poor.

Young people, women, and children are living in poverty, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has missed many opportunities to ensure a guaranteed annual income by reforming the welfare system. Nor has child care been discussed in the broader context of the poverty of Canada's young families.
These women and children wonder, in view of the fact that the poor of our country are unlikely to be adequately heard, insofar as welfare and child care are concerned what reforms does the Government have to offer which will be specifically targeted to the young people and the women and children of our society?

What has the Conservative Government done and what does it plan to do to change this unfair situation and to give families and children in this country the right to live in equality and justice?
April 21, 1988

Mr. Speaker, the right to own property, singly, jointly, or in a group, is one of the strengths of democracy. This right distinguishes a democratic country from all brands of totalitarianism and socialism that believe in the state owning all land.
Thousands of Canadians who came from other countries came to Canada because of their desire to own land, their own home, their own farm. The right to own property is part of the Canadian heritage. Why is this fundamental right not included in the Canadian Charter of Rights?
In 1981, because of the efforts of the PC Members, it was in the Charter for 48 hours, but during the weekend the Liberals caved in to the demands of the NDP and took it out, to their everlasting shame.
The Canadian Real Estate Association, the Canadian Bar, and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce all, along with most Canadians, want the right to own property enshrined in the Constitution. So let's put it in!

Mr. Speaker, today is the fortieth anniversary of the creation of the State of Israel, a nation based on religion and democracy. Created out of the chaos of World War II, it was a deliberate attempt by the United Nations to a find a homeland for a displaced people. Then, as now, the desire for peace and security from violence demanded tolerance, understanding, and good will.
We offer our congratulations today to Israel, believing that Israel and its neighbours will some day find that elusive solution to their problems by applying their genius, tolerance, and imagination. Then all peoples of the area will be able to celebrate peace.
It is all too easy for Canadians with our vast, thinly populated spaces to have difficulty understanding the problems of a part of the world heavily populated with many nationalities. However, today Canadians wish to congratulate Israel and offer our best wishes for peace and happiness.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Mr. Speaker, I first wish to thank you and Hon. Members from all three parties who defied custom and let me speak.
Today, the arts community is in mourning. Canada has lost a man of the theatre whose talent, versatility, devotion and leadership marked an era and will continue to have an impact on the whole Canadian arts community.

As Jean Gascon was preparing yet another production at the Stratford Festival, sadly the curtain fell and Canada's artistic community is in mourning.

From the Compagnons de Saint-Laurent to the Theatre du Nouveau-Monde, from the National Arts Centre to the Stratford Festival and the National Theatre School, artists and craftspeople have been enriched by their contacts with Jean Gascon.
To his wife, children and whole family, we extend our deepest sympathy.
Companions in good times and bad, disciples, students, patrons, and all of us in the general public will never let the flame he passed on to us die. Jean Gascon was a great artist and like all great artists, by making us laugh or cry, he made us better.
Thank you, Jean!

April 21, 1988

[DOT] (M05)

Mr. Speaker, during National Volunteer Week, I would like to pay tribute to all those Canadians who give so generously of their time for the benefit of their fellow citizens and their country. Across Canada this week, people are praising the invaluable contribution made by volunteers to the quality of our lives here in Canada. Their unselfishness has made us more compassionate and has made our cities and towns a good place to live.
Volunteer work is done in practically every sector of our society, including health care and social services, recreation, the arts, the environment and community development. Many volunteers are active in social work, making Canadians aware of the injustice and disparities present in our society.
Volunteer work is so much a part of our lives in this country that we often take it for granted. However, it deserves to be mentioned as one of the social forces that sustain our communities and as a source of national pride. Only through public recognition of the essential role played by volunteers in Canada can volunteer work continue to expand. Without their efforts, Mr. Speaker, the country would lose one of its fundamental characteristics: the spirit of solidarity and mutual assistance.

subsubtopic: NECHAKO HYDRO AGREEMENT-ALCAN'S REFUSAL TO APPEAR BEFORE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Alcan refused to appear before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans this week to answer questions about the Nechako hydro agreement signed last fall and has now been ordered to do so by all Parties represented on the committee. The agreement puts at risk 53 per cent of the sockeye habitat of the entire Fraser River system, will lower the natural flows of the Nechako to as little as 6 per cent of its volume, and will lower the Fraser River itself by three feet at some times of the year.
Alcan has been placed above the law and above Parliament through this agreement with the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon), insulated from public inquiry and scrutiny. It is unprecedented in Canada for a Cabinet or a Parliament to concede such constitutional powers to a private corporation. Rather than defend the rights of Parliament to set water flows necessary to protect fish, the Minister chose to impose an adverse water flow regime upon a common property resource for the private benefit of Alcan, not the public.
In British Columbia a province-wide coalition has taken this matter to the Federal Court, having filed just last week, and plans to fight all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada for justice and for Canada.

Fear not, children of Canada, for Robin Hood is still alive and well.
He wears not a cloak of green but a tie of red.
He lives not in Sherwood Forest, but at Queen's Park.
He leads not merry men, but a pack of thieves.
They rob, not from the rich but from everyone in Ontario.
They give not to the poor, but squander, squander, squander.
His name is not Robin, but Peterson, and his band calls itself Liberals.
Yesterday the people of Ontario again saw the effects of electing a Liberal Government which is irresponsible in its fiscal outlook and learned everything it knows from its federal Liberal cousins.
A Conservative Government in Ottawa is now attempting to correct the Grit years of mismanagement of Canada. The people of Ontario will not soon forget how they were hoodwinked by Peterson and his band of merry spenders.

April 21, 1988

Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of many other Members of the House to pay tribute, on the 40th anniversary of the creation of the State of Israel, to a remarkable country and a remarkable group of people who, over that 40 years, made great achievements in establishing a democratic system of government in the Middle East and in undertaking a number of important initiatives in science, technology, education, culture, and economics.
I think that Canadians have always felt a strong affinity for Israel, and throughout the years have clearly established our support for the existence of the State of Israel and its future. We all recognize that Israel is now going through a serious time of trouble and turbulence. I think all Members of the House reach out to that country and its neighbours in the hope their future will be far less troublesome than it is at present.
On behalf of my caucus and, I hope, other Members, I say congratulations to Israel on its 40th anniversary, and we look forward to another 40 years and more. To quote the Talmud, which I think represents the spirit of Israel,"if we can save one life, we save the whole world". I think that should be the standard we apply to the State of Israel and the situation it is now facing in its time of trouble.

speakeroldname: Hon. John W. Bosley (Don Valley West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most of us have experienced a 40th birthday. We know, Sir, that whether that event is traumatic or positive, it is a time when one takes stock of what one has achieved and what one hopes to achieve. Today is of course a very special birthday, for today Israel is indeed 40 years old, only 40 years old.
Whatever one thinks of Israel's policies, and one does not have to agree with all of them, no one can visit Israel without being utterly staggered by what she has achieved in such a short time. From desert to orange groves, her industrial, cultural, social and economic achievements have been miraculous. No other country in the world has achieved so much in 40 years. To have done all that in what has been far too often a war zone is only that much more impressive.
Israel is younger than most of us. Her people deserve even more our congratulations and the sure knowledge that we
continue to support their right to exist within secure borders. Perhaps we could paraphrase an old saying which is appropriate to this day and say let us pray, Sir, that "peace begins at 40".

Mr. Speaker, the Government's expensive scheme to buy nuclear submarines is dying the death of a thousand cuts. Expert after expert around the world is questioning the cost and the very reason for this program.
Jane's, perhaps the most respected voice on defence matters in the world, has just published the latest condemnation in a book by Anthony Cordesman who says "the true cost would be at least twelve billion." He warns that the horrendous cost of nuclear submarines "would mortgage Canadian defence investment funds for a generation." Mr. Cordesman is not alone.
Last week, Frank Gaffney from the Hudson Institute pointed out that the Government has not told Canadians about the total cost of operating and maintaining nuclear submarines. In fact, he even called them "obsolete death traps".
The chorus of experts condemning the nuclear submarine program is getting louder and louder. The question is: will the cold warriors in the Government listen?

subsubtopic: CANFOR CORPORATION-DISCOVERY OF COMPOUND TO REPLACE CHEMICAL SPRAYS
speechtext:

It is expected that lumber producers from around the world will want to use this product for the safety of their employees and customers.
