subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO END TOLLS ON CHAMPLAIN BRIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since 1984, I have taken every opportunity to mention the dissatisfaction of 40 million drivers who cross the Champlain Bridge each year with a situation that also discriminates against residents of the South Shore.

Now that the present Minister, formerly Minister of State, has the portfolio and, I hope, the power, we will finally be able to deal with the case of the toll on the Champlain Bridge that wastes hundreds of hours of work and hundreds of dollars worth of energy, and in the final instance yields very little to the Government of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I know the Government of Canada will have no choice but to end this discrimination. Why not do it now, because the people of the Eastern Townships and the South Shore should be able to go where they want without paying more than anyone else, and especially without wasting the amount of time they do now on the Champlain Bridge. Once again, I would urge the Government to meet the commitment it made in 1984, while there is still time!
The Socialist Party has already persuaded the unions to raise their dues to pay for the election campaign. Just think what it would cost the individual Canadian if a Liberal-Socialist coalition came to power!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We understand that he has been doing his best to downplay as much as possible the diplomatic storm between Canada and France.
Last Monday, in answer to a question in this House he went as far as to say, and I want to quote him precisely, that the negotiations on fisheries "have been continuing in an atmosphere of quite remarkable calm".

Since then I have been wondering where the Minister has been and who gave him the advice to stick his head in the sand.
Why have the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Government allowed our relationship with France to deteriorate to such a level that France has withdrawn her Ambassador, and our own outgoing Ambassador and yet unelected Secretary of State had this to say:
It is serious. If we don't take care it could be very serious.
It is not a sport. We cannot go on like this-escalation must stop
somewhere.
Perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs can try to square that with what he calls "calm negotiations".

Nuclear subs.

speechtext: A bunch of Gary Doers over there.

April 21, 1988

Mir. Howard McCurdy (Windsor-Walkerville): Mr. Speaker, I will repeat my question for the Prime Minister who made the promise. Is this to be another broken promise? Is the Prime Minister going to provide the $1.3 billion for the purposes for which he promised, or are we going to sneak some money away from the universities again for a project that, while everyone agrees is necessary, is in danger of affecting the entire Canadian scientific program?

Mr. Speaker, I tried to answer my hon. friend a few seconds ago but I was prevented from doing so. I am happy to try again. subtopic: LAY-OFFS AT MANITOBA CANADA PACKERS PLANT-NONPAYMENT OF BENEFITS

speechtext:

Oral Questions
Will the Prime Minister instruct his new Minister of Employment and Immigration to address immediately the serious inequity faced by those laid off workers at the Canada Packers plant, and ask for immediate redress so that they receive the same treatment as those who received salaries?

subtopic: LAY-OFFS AT MANITOBA CANADA PACKERS PLANT-NONPAYMENT OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend raises a very important problem in regard to the employees at Canada Packers. I will report back to the House just as quickly as possible.

If the Free Trade Agreement with the USA is implemented the grape industry in the Okanagan will be devastated. This is particularly unfortunate for your family-we have a responsibility to minimize risk in all loans we make.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-SITUATION OF OKANAGAN FAMILY
speechtext: Why after so many months is the Prime Minister unable to say in this House today exactly what it is going to do for the Somer family which will clearly lose its farm, its livelihood, and its well-being because of the Government's trade deal? After all the time he has had why can the Prime Minister not give a clear, definite, helpful, and meaningful answer today?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-SITUATION OF OKANAGAN FAMILY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend knows full well that with respect to an individual case having been raised I am incapable of responding directly to how that might take place in six months or a year. It is an individual case, and I will work with the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap in regard to that individual case.
If the Hon. Member wants to deal with substantial issues, he should look at the one million new jobs that have been created and the 250,000 new ones that will be created under the free trade deal, including the 30,000 new jobs that will be created in British Columbia alone over and above the important job-creation statistics that are ongoing in Canada. He should be pleased and celebrating that great fact here in Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Economic Council Report that he cited in his earlier response suggested that there would be far fewer jobs than the number he suggested, and I suggest that will continue.
That same report said that there had to be an adjustment program now to help those it admitted would be hurt by the Government's free trade deal.
Why has the Government failed to act on the advice of the very body it cites in support of its program? What is the use of talking about new jobs when it cannot point to the new jobs that it is going to give to even one family that will be hurt by the Government's trade deal?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the very report that the hon. gentleman refers to was very positive and very supportive of the free trade agreement.
I am sure all Members in the House will be delighted today to see that Ontario Hydro in its assessment of the deal states: "free trade will be a boon to at least the six largest electricity consuming industries in the province", and "the proposed pact will add a further 3 per cent to gross provincial product" in Ontario "over the next decade".
Oral Questions
That is a very positive assessment by Ontario Hydro right in the central province of Canada. Why does the hon. gentleman not open his eyes, and not just concentrate on the negative? The positives far outweigh the negative effects of this arrangement.

Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Finance. I am sure the Minister is aware that yesterday the Government of Ontario raised provincial sales and personal income taxes. This follows a disturbing trend set by Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island. All of these provincial Governments have, in the last few months, increased the sales and personal taxes of Canadians. Obviously, the Minister has failed to obtain consensus and co-operation from the provinces in regard to tax reform.
My question to the Minister is the following. Why did the Minister fail to anticipate this provincial tax grab, and why did he not secure provincial co-operation when he introduced tax reform?

Mr. Speaker, I do not think it will come as any surprise to the Hon. Member if I say that I am quite disappointed in the actions of the Ontario Government in its Budget yesterday. I think that this goes contrary to the direction that we have set out in tax reform where we are trying to get tax rates down for Canadians right across the board. This runs counter to that.
That's why it's not going to work.

If the Hon. Member wishes to look behind the reasons for this, he will find that the reason for the tax increase is the very high level of government spending in the Province of Ontario. It has been running at 9.5 per cent for four years now.
I should remind the Hon. Member that if Governments would follow the same course of action that his Party recommends of increasing spending successively year in and year out, that is the sort of response that we are going to see.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Hopefully, the Minister of Finance will also be in touch with Gary Lane, his colleague and friend in the Province of Saskatchewan. Because of his tax reform and what the Minister of Finance in Saskatchewan has done, the people of Saskatchewan are paying S22 million more in personal taxes. Obviously, Ontario residents face a net loss of some $286 million in tax savings.

April 21, 1988
Oral Questions
Will the Minister not admit today that he has failed in providing Canadians with fair tax reform? Will the Minister tell the House if he has been in contact with provincial Finance Ministers? If not, will he do so immediately and use his influence to find a solution to this disastrous situation? Canadian taxpayers are paying more and more every day.
Take it up with the provinces.
That's why your tax policy is not going to work. We have provinces.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know what more I can add to the question that the Hon. Member has put to me. The Hon. Member should look at the province next door to him which has been labouring under the burden of an NDP Government for a number of years. Last year there was a tax hit comparable to what we saw yesterday in the Province of Ontario, a tax hit that was unprecedented.
The type of thing that we have to be cautious about in government is to control government spending; keep the rate of growth of government spending under reasonable control, as we have in the federal Government where government spending has grown at a rate of approximately 4 per cent per annum for the period of time that we have been in office. It is that type of spending discipline which is the answer to the questions that the Hon. Member is posing. That is how we can get taxes down.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. When Cosmos 954 crashed in northern Canada 10 years ago, only five grams or one-tenth of one per cent of the deadly radioactive U-235 cargo was recovered. Two U.S. military bombers have crashed carrying plutonium, and when plutonium was released in Greenland 20 years ago, the clean-up cost $300 million. When plutonium was similarly released in Palmares, Spain, the clean-up cost $500 million.
What steps has the Minister of Transport taken to evaluate the safety of an emergency landing or the impact of an accident on northern Canada from the plutonium overflights of the Arctic by Japan which can begin next Monday?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister.
According to StatsCan data released yesterday, there has been a net regression in French outside Quebec, and if we read the information carefully, the fast rate of assimilation of a major group in our country makes it an endangered species.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister, considering the promise by the Premier of Saskatchewan to make Saskatchewan fully bilingual in fifteen years, how are we to reconcile the Premier's rather optimistic promise with this threat of assimilation?
How can he endorse and congratulate the Premier of Saskatchewan who is trying to evade the issue by having us believe that in fifteen years, Saskatchewan will be bilingual, although we know perfectly well that once there are no more Francophones in Saskatchewan, there is no way the province could be made bilingual?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's question concerns two issues. First of all, there is the Supreme Court's decision, and I have made it clear what my position and that of the Government was in this respect. I think it is substantially that taken by the Hon. Member. The first item is the Supreme Court's decision.
The second is the future of the Fransaskois. I think that for the first time, the Government of a Western province has said fairly and squarely that it intends to make a province that is now officially unilingual into a bilingual province sometime in the future, by taking concrete action.
As Prime Minister of Canada, I feel I must congratulate the Leader of this government and be prepared to co-operate with him in order to implement this new initiative intended to help the Fransaskois who, like other language minorities across this country, have been left to their own resources for nearly 90 years. I think we all have work to do at both levels, and perhaps at a third level as well, to help this language minority in Saskatchewan, and to protect its rights and enhance its prospects for the future.

CLOSURE OF AUTO PARTS PLANT IN WINDSOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Birla auto parts plant in Windsor has just been closed by its creditors, throwing 152 people out of work. A major cause, we have been told by officials of the Federal Business Development Bank, is the 10-cent increase in the value of the dollar over the last year.
Is the Minister of Finance finally prepared to admit that the increase in interest rates has been responsible for that increase in the value of our dollar and has killed this plant and thrown 152 people out of work?

subtopic: CLOSURE OF AUTO PARTS PLANT IN WINDSOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is drawing a very narrow conclusion about the cause of this situation. I have a good deal of sympathy for the people who work at that plant but if I were to be honest with them I would have to say that if that operation cannot make money with the dollar at the current level, there are other things wrong with it.
We have lived for a few years now with a dollar that was somewhat undervalued. That gave a new lease on life for some of those companies that were probably not competitive. However, we believe the level of the Canadian dollar reflects the strength of the Canadian economy and the increased level of activity here.
I should point out to the Hon. Member that in each of the last three or four months our trade surplus has increased so that we are demonstrating in a broad sense an ability to deal quite effectively with the level of the Canadian dollar at the position it is today.

The House resumed from Tuesday, April 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-117, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity as a western Canadian to say a few words this afternoon about this Bill. While it is an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act, in short a Bill to impose certain taxes, it is of significant importance to farmers across Canada, particularly many in western Canada.
There are a number of changes in this Bill, among which is an increase in the price of gasoline of 1 cent a litre. As Members will know, that increase took effect on April 1 despite the fact that this Bill had not been passed. However, until the Bill is passed the Government cannot rebate the 1 cent a litre tax on gasoline to prairie farmers.
Obviously a lot of us are very concerned about the small vendors who will sell gasoline products to farmers without charging the tax and then have to apply to Revenue Canada to get the rebate back to the dealer. We are similarly concerned about farmers who buy from very small retail dealers where the farmers apply for the rebate. The Bill is still in the House, it has not been sent to committee, and these small dealers are unable to claim the 1 cent rebate.
In western Canada it is a little drier than it usually is at this time of year and many farmers are making their plans for spring seeding. In fact, in many areas of the prairies, farmers are already actively working the land. This is a time when they consume a great deal of fuel. It is of significant concern to a lot of farmers that they must await passage of this Bill before they can claim their rebate.

Madam Speaker, needless to say the Official Opposition is somewhat surprised at the move by the Hon. Member. He purports to move the motion because of his concern about the rebate of the excise tax which went into effect on April 1, 1988. Perhaps he has not taken the opportunity to read the legislation, so 1 will remind him that if you do not increase the tax there is no necessity to give a rebate.
It took effect on April 1.

You cannot speak out of both sides of your mouth. The Hon. Member says that these tax increases have social value. He went on to say that they have social merit. How strange for him to be making those comments about a Bill amending the Excise Tax Act, especially in view of the comments made by certain members of his Party prior to the last election.
We all remember that during that particular election campaign, the Finance Minister (Mr. Wilson) made certain comments and certain promises. 1 would like to remind you, Madam Speaker, Hon. Members in the House, and indeed all Canadians, of some of the comments made by the Finance Minister, the Member for Etobicoke Centre, and some comments made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) himself.
For example, on March 6, 1984, when he was on this side of the House, the Finance Minister said:
We will reduce spending. We will refrain from increasing taxes, which are
already too high.
This was a promise made by the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre as a representative of the Conservative Party. He
promised the people of Canada that a Conservative Government would not increase taxes because taxes were already too high. What did the Conservative Government do from the moment it took office? Well, time is too short this afternoon to list all the taxes that have been implemented by the Government, but I would like to mention just a few.
In the February 1987 Budget there was a 12 per cent increase on snack foods and ice cream effective July 1, 1987. There was a 4 per cent increase in tax on cigarettes and tobacco effective February 19, 1987. There was a $4 per ticket increase in tax on air transport effective May 1, 1987, and August 1, 1987. There was an increase in sales tax on leaded and unleaded gasoline effective April 1, April Fool's Day, 1987. That was his February Budget, and we all remember that he said, "We will not raise taxes".
Let us look at some other tax measures implemented by the Government through the Minister of Finance, the June and December 1987 tax reforms. What did the Government do in those particular measures? There was a 10 per cent tax imposed on long distance telephone calls. When Canadians are paying their telephone bills and see that there is a 10 per cent tax, they should be reminded that this tax was introduced by the man who told Canadians that they were already paying too much in taxes, the guy who promised that he would not increase taxes.
Not only did he implement that tax in the June and December 1987 tax reform measures, he also increased the tax on paint and wallpaper from 8 per cent to 12 per cent. He increased the tax on alcohol and tobacco from 15 per cent to 18 per cent.
I am not criticizing the fact that Governments must at times raise taxes in order to meet expenditures. That is understandable as long as there is fairness and equity and the burden is equally shared among all segments of society. However, we on this side of the House take great exception to the fact that Members opposite seem to be speaking out of both sides of their mouths. What they say depends on whether they are in Government or in Opposition, whether they are speaking to a group in Ontario or a group in Prince Edward Island, or whether it is during an election campaign or it is said as Minister of Finance.
Let us look at another tax initiative introduced by the Minister of Finance. In the February 1988 Budget, he increased excise tax on motor fuels by 1 cent per litre. The list goes on, Madam Speaker, notwithstanding the Minister's promise not to increase taxes.
That was the Finance Minister. What did the Prime Minister have to say a few short years ago? On November 29, 1984, the Prime Minister said:
April 21, 1988

Canadians pay a good deal of money for government services and feel that
they are already paying quite enough.
That was a fair comment by the Prime Minister three and a half years ago. If he meant what he said on November 29, 1984-although his actions and those of his Government suggest that perhaps he did not really mean what he said- why did he allow his Finance Minister to introduce three or four Budgets resulting in substantial tax increases which hit low and middle-income earners more than higher income earners and corporations?
They made promises and they broke promises. These were not the only promises that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance made during that election campaign. We all know of the many promises they made and the many promises they have broken. During the election campaign three and a half years ago they also promised to share the tax burden across the board and reduce personal income tax. Let us examine the record of the Government vis-a-vis its Budgets over the last three and a half years and the increase in taxation.
In terms of budget revenues, from fiscal year 1984-85 to fiscal year 1988-89 personal income taxes were increased by a total of $15.1 billion, a 55 per cent increase. Compare that, if you will, to the increase in the corporate income tax. In fiscal year 1984-85 the increase was $9.4 billion, and in fiscal year 1988-89 it will be $12 billion, an increase of 28 per cent or $2.6 billion. A 28 per cent increase in corporate income taxes and a 55 per cent increase in personal income taxes hardly seems fair, not only because of the promises made by the Government during the election campaign, but also because of comments made by the Government throughout the last three and a half years. One questions the fairness and equity in increasing personal income taxes by 55 per cent and increasing corporate taxes by only 28 per cent. One can see from these figures that the increases have not been fair across the board.
In moving his motion the Member indicated that the excise tax increase on gasoline which went into effect on April 1, 1988, was of social value and social merit. The reason for moving his motion was to allow the rebate to be made to the farmers in western Canada more quickly. However, he does not tell the farmers in western Canada that the rebate is only given because of the tax increase itself. If he was truly concerned about the farmers in western Canada he would not vote for this particular measure which increases the tax not only on gasoline but on a number of other products and goods.
As I indicated, Bill C-117, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act is a rather lengthy Bill of 70 or 80 pages which contains a number of measures which would give lawful authority to some of the tax measures which were announced in the 1987 and 1988 Budgets and in the tax reform Ways and Means motions of June and December, 1987. Most of the main revenue- raising items in this piece of legislation have already been implemented, with the exception of one or two items. These revenue-raising items are some of the tools used by the Government to create its smoke and mirrors illusion. We know that during the election campaign
Excise Tax Act
the Conservative Party promised the people of Canada that they would reduce the deficit. That is fair enough, but one would have hoped and expected that the Government would have decreased the deficit by honest means.
I submit that it has used the smoke and mirrors illusion to lead the Canadians into believing that the deficit has in fact been decreased. The fact is that it has used certain measures not only at the expense of the average Canadian's wallet, but has used certain accounting techniques to reduce the deficit simply on paper.
I want to talk very briefly about the acceleration of federal excise and tax remittances and the manufacturers' sales tax. The Government has used the acceleration of federal sales tax and excise tax remittances as a method to have people believe that the $29.3 billion deficit the Government has been speaking about is lower than it actually is.
It bears repeating that one of the ways this illusion was created was with the use of accounting tricks such as the acceleration of federal sales and excise tax remittances. Canadian employers, who must deduct income tax, unemployment insurance premiums and Canada Pension Plan contributions from their employees and remit these deductions to the Government, have been required to do this more often since 1987. In effect, rather than remitting the federal income tax, Canada Pension Plan contribution and unemployment insurance contribution once a month, the Government has required the employers in Canada to remit them more often. In effect, it is getting money a little earlier than it otherwise would have received it and thereby affecting the cash flow of a lot of small businesses across the country. It does not represent an actual decrease in the deficit but is a trick to lead Canadians into believing the deficit is that much lower. It is only delaying an increase in the deficit.
In January, 1987, employers were remitting once a month. Now they are remitting twice a month. This gave the Government a one time only increase in revenue of $1.6 billion.
The Government then told employers to remit the deductions weekly, resulting in another increase in revenue for the Government. Due to the fact that the payroll deductions based on the new tax rates will not begin until July this year, the Government gives itself a six-month interest-free loan for this year, amounting to about $1 billion. That is another trick used by the Government to have Canadians believe the deficit is lower than it actually is.
The manufacturers' sales tax was dubbed by the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre, the Minister of Finance, as "the silent killer of jobs". Between October 1, 1984, and April 1, 1986, this tax increased from 9 per cent to 12 per cent because of his tax measures, notwithstanding the concerns he expressed when he was a member of the Opposition. This particular tax increase resulted in a $3 billion gain to the Government.

Manufacturers, too, are being required to remit this tax earlier, sometimes even before they have collected the tax from sales.
The Government continues to tinker with this tax, apply it to more goods, broaden the base, and increase the rates. Evidently, this will continue because the national sales tax with which the Government was going to replace it will not be presented before the next election.
The Government said in 1984 that it would not raise taxes, but it has proceeded to do so. Canadians take great exception to the fact that these tax increases have not been fair across the board. We all remember the first Budget that was handed down by the Minister of Finance in the spring of 1985, shortly after the election campaign. That was the Budget in which the Government tried to deindex senior citizens' pensions.
Who will forget the election campaign in the summer of 1984 when the Prime Minister referred to senior citizens' pensions as "a sacred trust"?
Canadians took him at his word, but when he came to office and the Minister of Finance brought down his first Budget, he tried to deindex senior citizens' pensions. The Government tried to reduce the deficit on the backs of senior citizens in Canada, thousands of whom are at or near the poverty line. The House will recall that in the very same Budget the Government gave a $500,000 capital gains exemption to the wealthy in society. In effect, it was a pure out and out gift of $125,000 to the wealthy in society.
To their friends.

To the Bay Street boys who support the Prime Minister.
I have outlined some of the income tax increases implemented by the Government. It has also used a number of other tricks to try to reduce the deficit. If it were not for the Opposition in the House of Commons and senior citizens from one coast to the other, that measure to deindex senior citizens' pensions would have been implemented. Because of the Opposition, the Minister of Finance and the Government were forced to back down. However, they did not back down from the deindexing of family allowances, personal credits and income tax tables. The Government proceeded with those measures by tricking Canadians. Rather than increasing taxes directly in this regard, it raised $635 million by deindexing some measures that Canadians have had as part of their income tax system for a number of years. These were measures that were meant to protect Canadian taxpayers from the ravages of inflation.
Other measures introduced by the Government include the elimination of the tax abatement, effective January 1, 1986, which was intended to raise $650 million. There was the elimination of the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, which was a very successful plan that was implemented by the previous Liberal administration. That plan was used by
thousands of Canadians in order to assist them in purchasing their first home. It was obliterated by the Government, effective May 27, 1985. By so doing, it saved $105 million.
The Government also put a temporary surtax on high-income earners of 5 per cent and 10 per cent, effective July 1,
1985,	to December 31, 1986. However, it slapped on top of that a permanent 3 per cent surtax on all taxpayers, including low-income earners.
It also implemented changes in the tax treatment of dividend income. Those tax changes were effective January 1,
1986.	It also changed spousal exemptions, which took effect January 1, 1986, to save the Government $20 billion.
In closing let me say that the Government has been somewhat less than forthright and honest with the people of Canada. As I indicated, promises were made and promises were broken. We in the Opposition have attempted to remind Canadians of those broken promises by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance with regard to taxation. It seems to me it is not too much to ask of politicians to follow through on their promises, although it might be too much to ask of Conservative politicians.

Madam Speaker, it was with interest that I listened to the comments of the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata). Indeed, the Member made some excellent points in this debate, especially in relation to the aggressiveness of the sales tax and how the Conservative Party, since being elected in 1984, has increased the tax burden on average Canadian families, particularly the middle and lower income earners.
I was dismayed, however, with respect to the Budget introduced last night in Queen's Park. I would have thought that the Liberal Party in Ontario would at least sing from the same hymn book as the Liberal Party in the House of Commons. The Liberal Party in Ontario has increased the sales tax by 1 per cent, from 7 per cent to 8 per cent. It also increased income tax by one point with another point increase next year.
The Ontario taxpayer would have been paying $450 million less because of the tax reform proposals. Now it will only be saving $164 million. What we are finding is that the provinces have been increasing their taxes, the tax rates have been going up, while the federal tax rate has in fact gone down because of tax reform, but at the same time the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) reduced the federal tax rates, he made up for it by increasing the sales tax. Now the provinces are increasing their part of the income tax rate as well as increasing their sales tax, so really what is happening is the poor taxpayers caught between provincial Finance Ministers and the federal Minister of Finance are being picked clean. I wonder if the Hon. Member would want to comment on what happened in Ontario last night.
April 21, 1988

1 would be pleased to comment, Madam Speaker. As the Hon. Member knows, all the provinces in Canada are suffering as a result of the tax measures introduced by this Government. Provincial governments have found themselves in the last several years with less revenue from the federal Government under the Established Programs Financing Act. This federal Government has reduced the transfer payments which would otherwise have gone to the provinces, including Ontario, which was especially hard hit by these drastic decreases in federal transfer payments for education and health care.
Billions and billions of dollars have not been transferred to the provinces because of the Government's tax measures, so the Province of Ontario was put in a position where it had to increase certain taxes. I would certainly ask the Hon. Member to understand some of the reasons certain tax measures were necessary in the Province of Ontario and also to examine that particular Budget as a package to see how the Government of Ontario has effectively assisted those low and middle income earners, more so than the wealthier in society.
The Hon. Member also has to consider some of the expenditures announced in that particular Budget. For example, I am sure he agrees with the increase of $300 million for education in the Province of Ontario. When one looks at the tax measures introduced in the Budget, one also has to look at the expenditures. It would be my respectful submission that the Budget handed down by the Treasurer of the Province of Ontario is a fair and equitable Budget, unlike the Budgets handed down by this Government.

Madam Speaker, first, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) for having made a very thoughtful and well reasoned speech in the House of Commons today. The Member will know, as I do, that the free trade agreement has been well advertised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) as having one very worthwhile redeeming feature, if nothing else was good about it. According to the Prime Minister, this particular free trade agreement would result in lower tariffs. Therefore, when Canadians purchase goods made in the United States of America, presumably these goods would be cheaper. However, the last Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), supported by his Prime Minister, presented to Canadians an increase in the price of gasoline. There was an equal reduction in the amount of revenues generated by tariffs on products imported into Canada. That leads me to believe that in fact what we have done is increased the price of gasoline to pay for the reduction of tariffs.
Would my colleague not agree that that being the case, this so-called free trade deal can be considered anything but free, particularly because what we have allegedly saved in the right hand we will now be paying out from the left hand? Is it not a little less than honest of the Government to pretend that Canadians will be saving money because of free trade when such is not the case?

Madam Speaker, there is no doubt at all that Canadians will be made to pay for the so-called free trade agreement. As my colleague pointed out, it is really not a
Excise Tax Act
"free" trade agreement. Canadians are receiving nothing for free. They in fact will have to pay for this pet project of the Prime Minister, if ever this particular agreement is ratified by Parliament.
It was hidden in the last Budget handed down by the federal Government. It was not something the Minister of Finance stood up and spoke about. It was tucked away in the many documents given to us when the budget was handed down. Tucked away was the fact that lower tariffs would result in lower revenues for the Government. Just by some strange coincidence, or what might appear to be a strange coincidence, the amount of dollars the Canadian Government would not receive because of the reduction in tariffs happens to be exactly the same amount Canadians would be asked to pay through the increase in the price of gasoline. That might appear to some to be coincidental, but I am sure the Minister of Finance and his colleagues sat around the cabinet table and asked themselves: "We are not going to get as much money as we otherwise might get without free trade. It is going to cost us. Let's stick it to Canadians through the Excise Tax Act by increasing the price of gasoline".
I hope the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake will remind his constituents, his farmers, that it is because of the free trade agreement that the excise tax on gasoline has increased. Had it not been for the free trade agreement with the United States, this particular tax increase might not have been necessary, in which case there would be no need to provide a rebate.
In reply to the question put by my hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), who always asks direct and forthright questions, yes, the bottom line is that this particular Bill, Bill C-117, which provides amendments to the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act, has some ramifications so far as the free trade agreement with the United States is concerned.

Madam Speaker, I too wish to participate in this debate this afternoon. The Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Gormley) has introduced a motion which states that the question be now put with respect to Bill C-117. This certainly gives me another opportunity to make some comments on the Bill.
When I think of all the manoeuvres taken by the present Conservative Government in the area of taxation, Bill C-117 clearly indicates the record of the Government. In many ways the Conservative Party and its Government make claims that they have reduced the taxes of large numbers of Canadians through tax reform, a piece of legislation which we have yet to see. The fact is that many of those dollars that Canadians will get back in terms of reduced tax rates because of tax reform the Government has already taken back through increasing the sales tax.

April 21, 1988
Excise Tax Act
To unscrupulous politicians the sales tax is a beautiful tax. It is a tax that is hardly noticed. It is the nickel and diming tax. It is the tax that one pays every time one buys a chocolate bar. So many cents go to the federal Government because of the federal sales tax that the Conservative Party slapped on kids' chocolate bars, soft drinks and popsicles. Every time they go to the corner store to spend part of their allowance on a popsicle they, too, will be helping to reduce the national deficit so to speak. They, too, will be paying part of their allowance to the federal Treasury in terms of taxes on popsicles, soft drinks, chocolate bars and ice cream cones.
People who have pets will be contributing to the national coffers when they go to buy pet food or kitty litter. The Government has imposed as well a sales tax on cat food, dog food, canary feed, cat litter and so forth. The kid who goes out to buy himself or herself a kite or a model airplane will be contributing to the national coffers since the Government has decided to tax those items as well.
Those who live in rural and remote communities and who have to place long distance telephone calls to their friends or family in the town next to them will also be paying new taxes, thus adding to the federal coffers. One move the Government has taken is with respect to slapping on a 10 per cent tax on communications. I will have more to say about that later on in my speech.
What we have is a Government that on the one hand is claiming to have reduced personal income tax rates while on the other because of tax reform, it is taking almost all of that back as a result of increasing the sales tax, the hidden tax, the sneaky tax as I call it.
Even the claim that the Government has made that it has reduced income taxes on the vast majority of Canadians is something that also has to be taken into context. When we compare what those Canadians will be paying after tax reform we see that it will still be more than what they were paying before the Tories came into power.
When the Tories claim that they reduced taxes and the number of people on the tax rolls, they do not compare it with 1984 when they were elected. They just compare it to the previous year. Thus what we have is the Tories coming into power in 1984 and every year that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has stood up on budget day we have seen different tax increases. In fact, Canadians did not even have to wait for budget night to find tax increases. They also found them every other time the Minister of Finance stood up to make an economic statement. Invariably, he took the opportunity to slap another tax on the taxpayers of Canada.
What we find in terms of the Tory record starting from 1984 is steady tax increases every year. Let me read into the record what some of those are. The main revenue raising item in the Bill before us is a 10 per cent tax on telecommunications services, such as telephone and telex services but not including charges for local residential telephone lines. That measure was announced in the June, 1987, White Paper.
As I mentioned before, this tax discriminates against people in northern and remote communities as well as in rural communities. There are parts in my constituency of Regina
East in which people pay long distance rates to call their doctor who might live in the town next to them. These people will be charged 10 per cent on those calls. It is a charge that people living in urban centres will not have to pay. Surely, the strength of this country is also its rural areas. We have a vast country, and in many ways it is underpopulated. Surely, it should be government policy to encourage people to live in our rural areas, the small towns, villages and hamlets of Canada. Instead, what we find when sales taxes such as the telecommunications tax are imposed is that people who live, in our small towns, our hamlets and our villages are being penalized.
The same can also be said for the many increases the Government has introduced on the gasoline tax. Let us consider that history.
In 1984, the economic statement increased the price of oil and gas which meant $100 extra would be paid per year by the average family. As well, in November of 1984, after barely two months in office, the Government introduced sales tax increases and other increases, such as increases in the unemployment insurance premium, which totalled an increase for the average Canadian family of some $352 per year. Then, a few months later, on May 23, 1985, the Minister of Finance brought down his first Budget. It contained various tax measures which meant that the average taxpayer after that day ended up paying some $512.50 more in taxes. Thus we had to pay $352 more in taxes in November, 1984.
In May of 1985 we saw a further increase in taxes of $512.50. As well in that statement we saw that the gas tax was increased. A few months later, on June 27, 1985, before the parliamentary break for summer, the Minister of Finance rose in the House to increase again the taxes that Canadian taxpayers would be paying. That day cost the average Canadian family some $340 in extra taxes per year. Again, there was a 1 per cent increase on gasoline.
A few months later, on February 18, 1987, the Minister of Finance introduced a Budget. There was again a further tax increase on gasoline, as well as increases in the sales tax, cigarette tax and so forth. That day cost the average family some $65 to $100 extra in taxes per year.
We also find that not too long ago, on February 10 of this year, the Minister of Finance stood in the House to increase the tax on gasoline by one cent per litre. That cost the average Canadian family some $50.
In every one of his economic statements or Budgets the Minister of Finance has increased the tax on gasoline. That discriminates against my rural constituents. People who live in the rural areas of Canada and who need to drive their cars longer distances to go to visit their dentist, to go shopping or to visit family will be paying more in taxes than Canadians living in larger urban centres. The tax on communications and the tax on gasoline is a direct disservice and a disincentive for Canadians who live in the rural areas of this great country of ours. It is darn poor policy planning on the part of the Government, and it is a crime what it is doing to the rural areas of Canada.
April 21, 1988

There is another aspect of the increase in sales taxes that should be mentioned in this debate. That is the effect that the Tory tax increases have had on inflation. It is common sense that as the tax is increased on goods and services, the price is increased that Canadians have to pay, and inflation is increased. Last year there was an inflation rate of some 4 per cent. If the Tory Government had not introduced all of the sales tax increases, that inflation rate would be closer to 2 per cent. A 2 per cent inflation rate is an acceptable inflation rate.
With an inflation rate of 2 per cent, interest rates could be reduced. A true inflation rate of 2 per cent would justify a 1 per cent drop in interest rates. A 1 per cent drop in interest rates would help young families struggling to get by and paying off their mortgage month after month. It would make life a little easier for them. It would give them a little more disposable income that they could spend on other goods and services, for example, going to the family restaurant on a weekend which, in turn, perhaps would allow the restaurateur to hire an extra waitress and create more employment.
A drop of 1 per cent in the interest rate would have a tremendous benefit on many farmers who live in my constituency. It would give them some relief on the payments that they have to make to service their farm debt. A decrease in the interest rates charged would have an economic benefit throughout the country.
The Minister of Finance and the Governor of the Bank of Canada have rejected our appeals for lower interest rates, appeals called for by various provincial Premiers, economic advisory bodies, and some of the banks. The Minister of Finance has told us in the House that it is bad economics to lower the interest rate because it would be inflationary. The Minister of Finance has stated that as long as inflation is at 4 per cent we cannot afford to drop that interest rate. I would suggest that if we are really interested in dropping the inflationary rate, then let us get rid of some of the sales taxes that have increased the inflation rate. In fact, the major reason that we have inflation in this country is because of the increases in the sales tax.
The other aspect that I wish to touch upon in this debate is the interrelationship between the sales tax increases and free trade. I noted that the spokesperson from the Liberal Party also made mention of this fact. When the Minister of Finance presented the Budget in February of this year, we again saw an increase in the sales tax on gasoline. Further on in the documents we noted the Minister stating that the Canadian public would save somewhere in the order of $300 million to $400 million because of the reduction in tariffs that would occur starting in 1989.
Excise Tax Act
When one looks at the number given by the Minister for the reduction in public revenues because of the elimination of certain tariffs, it is approximately the same as the revenue the Government was going to gather by increasing the sales taxes. That said it all. Under the free trade agreement we will see a certain reduction in some of the tariff items, which means decreased government revenues. The Government gave notice in the February Budget that those savings that Canadians will enjoy because of this agreement will be paid back to the federal Treasury in increased sales taxes. I submit that that is dishonest.
Let the Government at least be honest and state that while there will be a reduction in prices because of the elimination of some tariffs, the federal Treasury cannot afford the loss of that revenue and, therefore, it will be collecting it back from Canadians by increasing the sales tax, income tax, or by whatever means. But at least be honest. Do not play games with the people of Canada. They are tired of governments that promise one thing and say one thing and do the exact opposite. They want honest government that is up front.
If the Government can demonstrate that those revenues are needed, that it has done everything it can to reduce government waste and duplication, and that it is not in the pork barrel and squandering money on its friends and chums, then I think that the Canadian people would be prepared to accept hard economic reality and would be willing to put their shoulder to the wheel in a national effort to reduce the deficit.
Canadians get very angry when they find that games are being played on them, and with sleight of hand tricks that attempt to snatch an extra dollar out of their pockets; when they see patronage appointments and the squandering of public money; when they see that the burden of reducing the deficit is not properly and fairly shared, that the well-to-do and the large corporations are not paying their fair share. In fact, in many instances the large profitable corporations are not paying a cent of tax. I think that Canadians are angry and disgusted, and they have had enough with this Government.
Despite the promises of open, clean, and fair Government that the Tories made in the 1984 election, we have seen the Tories, as we saw the previous Liberal administration, with their snouts in the barrel or trough looking after their pals and their friends. There has been the continuation of an unfair tax system that benefits the rich and the well-to-do and fleeces the middle income earner, the low income earner, and the poor of this country.
That is why it is with pleasure that I participate in this debate today and urge the House to defeat the motion, and later to defeat the Bill itself.

April 21, 1988
Excise Tax Act

Madam Speaker, I have sat in the House for three and half years now and during all that time I have heard Members of the NDP sanctimoniously tell us that they have all the answers. There may be some people in Canada who believe some of the things that the NDP are saying. We in Manitoba have been able to judge the NDP by their actions as a government. Very briefly, I want to mention a couple of points.
The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) spoke about squandering of public money. In the past seven years, government expenditures were up 87 per cent in Manitoba. The debt has doubled, and 60 per cent of that is owed to foreigners.
What about taxes? In the past 12 months, there has been one of the largest tax grabs in Manitoba's history. The increased sales tax affects everyone. In the past 12 months, taxes to the middle class have increased in the neighbourhood of 25 per cent. There is a payroll tax of 2.25 per cent in Manitoba. Every employer in the province must pay 2.25 per cent on gross payroll. I call it an employment tax, the Manitoba Government calls it a payroll tax.
The Hon. Member talks of dishonesty. I would like him to tell me how he rationalizes what the NDP says about things like that and what it does when it is in Government.

Madam Speaker, I certainly thank the Hon. Member for the points he has raised. First, though, the Hon. Member neglected to mention the debt rate the NDP inherited from the previous Tory Government, left by the squandering of money and the inefficient programs that were undertaken in Manitoba at that time.
To be sure, Manitoba has gone through a rough period and continues to go through a rough period. The Government there made a decision to attempt to maintain a satisfactory level of employment and has conducted economic programs that have cost money.
I noted that in the Hon. Member's question he did not make any suggestion as to what programs the Manitoba provincial Government should have cut. I wish he would also look at the situation in the Province of Saskatchewan where there has been a Tory Government since 1982. That Government inherited a public treasury with a surplus, and it had been running with a surplus for years. Since that Government was elected, the Saskatchewan Tories have driven that province so far into debt that Saskatchewan now has the highest per capita debt in Canada, thanks to a Tory Government.
I could list a whole ream of programs that Government introduced that have been wasteful and have squandered public money. That Government continues to do that. Let me give you several examples of this, as so many come to mind.
Seeing that it was in some political difficulty, the Government of Saskatchewan made a very strategic decision to buy its re-election during the last provincial election of 1986. One
of the things it did was to offer every farmer in Saskatchewan $25 an acre at 6 per cent interest, whether they needed it or not, whether they were in difficulty or not, whether they farmed their land or not. The program was universal. Everyone got it and everyone took it.
We now hear of cases of people who did not need the money but took the $25 an acre at 6 per cent interest, turned it around and reinvested it at 10 per cent, 11 per cent or 12 per cent. They made themselves a tidy sum of money. That whole program cost the public treasury some $1 billion.
Now the Tories are trying to collect this money back. Of course, the farm situation has not improved. There are many farmers who are worse off today than they were when they got the $25 an acre. They are in no position to start paying that money back.
Now the Government of Saskatchewan is starting to patch together some programs. It is attempting in all sorts of ways to get this money back. Of course, it is creating divisions within the communities. The provincial Government might very well be in a position of having to force some farmers into bankruptcy just to try to get this money back.
That was a very irresponsible program, a program that was badly designed and badly thought out from a public administration point of view. Of course, that program's entire reason for being was the re-election of the Devine Government, and it was willing to spend $1 billion on it, increasing the public debt in Saskatchewan by $1 billion.
I see that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is leaving. The Minister knows, as I pointed out in the House earlier this week-I am sorry, I should not mention that the Minister of the Environment is present or is not present. In any event, I mentioned to the Minister earlier this week the project the Government of Saskatchewan wants to undertake. It wants to build a dam on the Souris River, a dam that will cost over $1.5 billion. This will create employment in the Town of Estevan in the Premier's riding, but that dam will depend entirely on run-off. It will create electricity that is more expensive than the electricity that can be bought from Manitoba or even from North Dakota. It makes no economic sense whatsoever, and environmentally, it is the most foolish idea. That is one of the driest parts of the province.
I understand that it was in 1912 when the water levels of the Souris River were first measured. Had the construction of that dam been finished in 1912, that body of water would not have filled up sufficiently to allow the generation of electricity until 1942. That is how much run-off water exists in that part of the province. Yet Mr. Devine is prepared to squander $1.5 billion of the money of Saskatchewan taxpayers just to ensure his reelection in his constituency of Estevan. That, I would suggest, is irresponsible public behaviour on the part of the Tory Government of the Province of Saskatchewan, and it is totally reprehensible.
April 21, 1988

Madam Speaker, it is obvious that the Tories do not want to hear about the tragic way in which they are trying to hoodwink Canadians. This legislation is typical Tory. It hits the poor, the weak, and the low income earner. Those with high incomes benefit. People like the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) have high salaries, so they have the big advantage. It is the poor ordinary Canadian, those who work in Canada's forest industry, the small entrepreneurs hauling wood in northern Ontario or northern New Brunswick, who are hurt by this legislation. All of these tax reform measures introduced by the Government are regressive in nature. The income tax rates have been pushed down, but who does that help? Mainly those in the upper income bracket.
On the CTV program Question Period in the spring of 1984 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said he would not have
Excise Tax Act
to increase taxes. He said he would be able to solve any deficit problem simply by cutting expenditures. He certainly did that. He cut everything in sight, from old age pensions to the deindexation of tax rates, research in agriculture, and he increased service charges. He did so in a dramatically more regressive way than any other Minister of Finance in history. The personal tax increases put in place between September 4, 1984, and the spring of 1987 represent the largest increase at any time in our history.
However, this is all part of a grand scheme. It is designed to hit hard early in the mandate of the Government and then give back a pittance toward the end. The Government has not got around to giving back the pittance, but we are told that a reduction in income taxes for the average Canadian of about $100 or $150 will take place around the end of July of this year.
It is interesting that the Government has been unable to reduce the deficit by any significant amount. The projected deficit was $30 billion and it is still $30 billion, yet over that period of time the Government increased personal income taxes by 16 per cent or some $22 billion.
It is not only the amount of taxes which is horrendous, it is the type of taxes. It is the senior citizen going to the drugstore to buy a non-prescription drug who will pay an extra 12 per cent. This adds up to $950 million on all prescription drugs. Then we have gasoline. If you live in western Canada or northern Canada where you have to drive maybe 60 or 100 miles to do your shopping or obtain health care or see a lawyer or whatever, you have to pay an extra 4 cents a litre for your gas. That is almost 20 cents a gallon. The Clark Government in 1979 increased the tax by only 18 cents a gallon and it was driven out after nine months. You can imagine what is going to happen to the present Government after four years and a 20 cent a gallon increase in gasoline taxes.
We also have to deal with the extremely regressive nature of these taxes. The increase in the sales tax alone amounts to 25 per cent. If you bought a television for $1,000 in 1984, you paid a $90 tax. Today you will pay $120 tax on that same item. That is just for openers. The Government has not revealed what its new super-duper sales tax is going to be. We hear snatches here and there of how it is going to work. For example, yesterday the Canadian Real Estate Board met here in Ottawa. One of its members described how the tax is going to work on a family buying a new home.
We read today how housing prices, especially in the area around Toronto, are going up dramatically. Let us say you buy a home for $100,000. The builder has paid perhaps $50,000 for materials. Under the proposed super-duper sales tax which the Minister of Finance forecast in his tax reform, if it is 10 per cent you will be paying a tax of $10,000 because you will be paying tax not only on the materials but also on the labour as well.

April 21, 1988
Excise Tax Act
We have to look at the approach the Government has used to justify the tremendous tax increases in every direction. Not only has it dramatically increased taxes, it has used every possible trick in the book to make its Budgets look great. It does not look that great to Canadians but it would look a lot worse, certainly to the Government's friends on Bay Street in Toronto, if it did not use all these tricks. For example, it sold Teleglobe, one of the very profitable Crown corporations and entered the money it received in last year's Budget projections to pull the deficit below $30 billion. As well, it speeded up the remittance of income tax, Canada pension and unemployment insurance remittances employers have to make, thereby giving itself a one-time windfall of about $1.5 billion. Little beknown to most Canadians, that is what is happening right now. They have imposed the new tax increases and do not actually have to reduce them until July.
We have this litany of tremendously regressive tax increases combined with all kinds of tax tricks which the Government has been using to try to make itself look good in spite of its very poor management of the economy and the fiscal framework of the country.

Madam Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity this afternoon to speak on the motion to put the question on Bill C-117. It gives me the opportunity to put on the record some of the consequences of Bill C-117 and also to draw, particularly in the light of last night's events, some interesting parallels between the direction in which the federal Government is heading and the direction in which the Government of Ontario is heading.
We know that the proposed outline for federal tax reform which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has put forward is generally quite good. Under that tax reform many taxpayers can look forward to savings. Were it my Party the Government introducing such a tax reform, we would not have distributed the savings disproportionately toward the upper end of income earners as has the Government. Nevertheless, there is an overall tax saving by way of the tax reform which is, of course, a reform of income taxation essentially in the order of $450 million.
We saw the parallel to Bill C-117 in Ontario last night, that is, that the federal Government and the Liberal Government in the Province of Ontario are determined to get those taxes back somehow. When we compare the litany of additional taxes, extension to taxes, and additional charges by way of excise and federal sales tax with the tax grab conducted by the Treasurer of Ontario, the Hon. Robert Nixon, last night, we will see some parallels in the way in which it is being done.
The 10 per cent tax on telecommunications services which is already being collected and which I believe has led to disproportionate taxation, particularly on the residents of my riding for whom most calls are long-distance calls rather than local calls, is one example of how the federal Government has
identified a new area not previously subject to taxation and has decided to dip the revenue ladle into that pool of funds.
It has, of course, already cost residents of Kenora-Rainy River dollars on their telephone bills. However, one area of service which I believe is particularly unfair to tax is radiotelephones. These normally rent for $50 and up per month, depending on a number of factors. The taxation of what is essentially a lifeline, because these are, of course, installed for people who cannot get normal pole line telephone service, to the tune of $5 or $10 a month before the long-distance calls are taxed, is an unfair impact of the Government's tax program.
The increase in taxation on telecommunication programming-cable and pay TV-from 8 per cent to 10 per cent has been remarked upon before. There has been an increase in tax on paint and wallpaper from 8 per cent to 12 per cent. There has been an acceleration of the remittances somewhat along the lines of the acceleration in the remittances of employee deductions. There has been an increase from 15 per cent to 18 per cent in the sales tax on beer, spirits, wines and tobacco. That is directly paralleled in the Ontario Budget. There is also the increase in the tax levy on air transportation and the increase in taxation on gasoline.
When we look at the parallels with the Province of Ontario it would seem, in the most daring tax grab in living memory by a provincial government, the Liberal Government of Ontario, that it has learned very well some of the lessons which the federal Government has taught. The sales tax is to go up by 1 per cent, from 7 per cent to 8 per cent. In Ontario a family of four is going to be facing a sales tax increase of $126 per year with no off-setting credits. Under federal income tax reform Ontario taxpayers would have saved $450 million. Of that $450 million saving, the Treasurer of Ontario, the grinch who stole spring, has taken that $286 million into the tax coffers of the province.
This poses a problem in designing tax systems in the country and raises the question of whether there should perhaps be more federal-provincial consultation before these changes are made. If one level of government reduces taxation in one area, which a province then moves in to occupy, at the same time as the federal Government is increasing taxation in the sales and excise tax areas, we have over-all higher taxation and the average taxpayer is hit with a double whammy, the provincial tax and the federal sales and excise taxes.
In addition to that the Treasurer of the Province of Ontario has, in two stages, raised provincial income tax by 2 per cent which, of course, is an effective increase in the tax yield to Ontario of 4 per cent. That will become effective in the 1988 and 1989 tax years.
I do not want to make any particularly detailed comment on the increases in the so-called sin taxes which we see in both Bill C-117 and the provincial Budget. However, the Governments together must recognize that there will be a point of diminishing returns.
April 21, 1988

Turning to the gasoline tax, the rate of increase by the federal Government under Bill C-117 is 1 cent a litre and the provincial Government in Ontario is taking an extra penny a litre on unleaded and an extra 4 cents a litre on leaded. I think that that is sheer tax opportunism on the part of the Liberal Government of the Province of Ontario. Surely it was not necessary to increase the tax rate on leaded gasoline by a full 4 cents per litre in order to get price parity between leaded and unleaded.
In my riding many people are still using leaded gasoline for their daily transportation. For example, there are people in some 27 communities in my riding which do not have road connections who use snowmobiles in the winter and outboard motor boats in the summer just to get around their communities. In addition, leaded gasoline is a necessity for those who have kept older vehicles.
I do not think that it was necessary for the province to jump that rate by 4 cents per litre. They should have recognized that it is simply a marketing situation. The leaded gasoline, while it is still available and still needed, is used as, so to speak, the fighting brand at the gasoline pump and is priced significantly lower. An increase in the order of 2.5 cents would have led to a rethinking of pricing structures by the petroleum companies and eventually to price parity between leaded and unleaded gasoline, which is surely what was desired. However, the Treasurer of Ontario went straight ahead and took 4 cents.
Another impact of that gasoline taxation is, of course, the phenomenon of ratcheting. Those of us who live in remote areas of the country, to where goods have to be transported over larger distances, end up paying higher prices and therefore, of course, higher taxes. A bedroom suite which would cost $900 in Toronto would cost $1,200 in the community of Red Lake. That means, of course, a contribution of one-third more by the taxpayer in Red Lake than by the taxpayer in Toronto.
Increases in the price of gasoline and the price of motor fuels that are used to transport the goods tend to ever increase that difference between the tax contribution made in the more remote parts of the country and the major centres.
I see that you are signalling that my time is up. I am glad to have had the opportunity to make these comparisons between this Government's tax grab and that of the Liberal Government in Ontario.
