Madam Speaker, I also welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate and to deal with a very important aspect of this administration.
Madam Speaker, I think it is important to go back to September 1984, when the Government took over the responsibility for the country's finances. At the time, Canada was
Excise Tax Act
coming out of an unprecedented recession which had obliged governments to take steps to ensure that Canadians would not suffer unduly from the consequences of this recession.
There was, of course, a substantial deficit which had to be dealt with after the election. Although by September 1984 the economy had started to improve quite considerably, decisions had to be made with a view to reducing the deficit.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to recall that this Government promised to substantially reduce the deficit and also to substantially reduce the tax burden on Canadians. At this point, it would be relevant to mention two comments. The first was made by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), who said on March 6, 1984 that they would reduce spending and refrain from increasing taxes that were already very high. Later in that same year, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that Canadians were paying a pretty penny for Government services and had the feeling they were paying enough.
Mr. Speaker, these two comments left the impression that the Government would deal with this tax burden by substantially reducing the amounts paid by Canadians which were already fairly high.
Today, the House is considering Bill C-117, whose purpose is to ratify substantial tax increases, most of which are already in effect and undermining Canadians' ability to pay.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to explain what this Government has done in the three and half years it has been running this country. I think that in the circumstances, it would have been normal for the Government to deal with the country's finances by going to those who are able to pay and to cope with these tax increases.
The Government did the exact opposite. It has been said many times and on many occasions that the tax burden had to be redistributed. In other words, improve the country's finances by letting those who are well off pay their share and provide relief for people on low incomes.
Today, in April 1988, we see that after three and a half years, revenues from sales tax and personal income tax increased by 55 per cent, while revenues collected from corporations increased 28 per cent.
We also see that revenues from sales tax and excise tax increased 77 per cent. The conclusion is that personal income tax and sales and excise tax increased far more than corporate taxes. I would like to get back to this later on.
Madam Speaker, we have here an administration that has constantly increased taxes since it came to power in 1984. This Government, instead of collecting the money where it is likely to find it, has taken the opposite stand and launched a cruel, savage and even obscene attack on the incomes of those who unfortunately have no way of escaping these systematic and on-going increases and are not able to cope with all these expenses-

April 21, 1988
Excise Tax Act
As you know, all indirect taxes are regressive. The low-income taxpayer tends to spend a larger share of his income on consumer goods. We all know that, and we all agree it is true. In 1986, the Government introduced a refundable sales tax credit. This credit is clearly inadequate, however, since it now totals $70 per adult and $35 per child. The cutoff point, after which the credit starts to go down was set at $16,000, well below the poverty line.
Madam Speaker, this proves beyond a doubt what the Government has indicated on many occasions, and that is its determination to make average Canadians whose ability to pay is certainly not able to absorb all these increases ... To prove that these increases are aimed especially at those who do not necessarily have the ability to absorb them, I shall, if I may, give a short summary of the tax increases we have seen since September 1984.
As far as indirect taxes are concerned, we have had repeated increases in sales tax: from 9 to 10 per cent on October 1, 1984, from 10 to 11 per cent on January 1, 1986, and from 11 to 12 per cent on April 1, 1986. These three increases in indirect taxes yielded $3 billion.
There was also the decision to extend sales tax to candy, soft drinks and snacks, with increases on July 1, 1985 and July 1, 1987, resulting in revenues totalling $460 million for the Treasury. We also had an increase in sales tax from 8 to 12 per cent on paint, wallpaper and toys, which yielded another $60 million. We had the increases in the excise tax on gasoline: 2 cents per litre on September 3, 1985, 1 cent per litre on January 1, 1987, 1 cent per litre on February 19, 1987, and 1 cent per litre on April 1, 1988, which yielded the princely sums of nearly $900 million and $450 million! Equalizing the sales tax on leaded and unleaded gasoline meant another $30 million. We also had progressive increases in the rate of airport taxes. The excise tax on alcohol and tobacco rose as well, yielding many hundreds of millions of dollars. Finally, the 10 per cent tax on long-distance calls and cable TV services, totalling $945 million.
Madam Speaker, these taxes have brought in billions of dollars in revenues and this entire burden has been assumed almost exclusively and fully by Canadian men and women with a very limited ability to pay. This is the trick which the Government used not really to reduce the deficit, but to increase the revenues in order to be able to claim openly: We have managed to slow down the rate of increase of Government expenditures.
That is not the point at all. The fact is that callously the Government has very heavily taxed Canadian men and women to secure considerably higher revenues.
Also, indirect taxes have been shamefully increased by the Government. Furthermore family allowances, personal credits and income tax deductions were de-indexed effective January 1, 1986, which brought in as much as $635 million in tax revenues. The elimination of the tax abatement brought in $650 million in additional revenues; the elimination of the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan deduction: $105 million; the 5-10 per cent temporary surtax on high income earners, the only one which could be acceptable because it is
aimed at high income earners, Madam Speaker, brought in $500 million in a context of several billion dollars. There was the permanent 3 per cent surtax on all taxpayers which brought in $1.2 billion; there were the changes in the tax treatment of dividend income, and finally in the spousal exemption, which saved the Government $20 million.
Madam Speaker, this is clear evidence that the Government is determined to place the tax burden on the backs of low and middle income taxpayers, when it should use this opportunity to work on a fair, equitable and harmonious tax reform and thus those with the ability to pay could share in the deficit reduction effort.

Madam Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to speak to Bill C-117 which, of course, is intended to give legislative effect to a number of federal sales tax and excise tax increases and excise duty changes announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). This legislation calls attention to the characteristics of the sales tax which recommend it and similar taxes to this Government. It, of course, has a number of advantages, one of which is it is simple to administer.
Another attractive aspect of the sales tax is it is hidden. The ordinary citizen does not really know how much it is costing him or her. It is a tax which is completely consistent with the character of this Government. It is a tax to be implemented by this Government for one simple reason, it is sneaky and perfectly consistent with the approach the Government has chosen to use with the Canadian people. The Government's way to get money from the taxpayers is to be a pick-pocket rather than be up front in arranging things so people will be fully conscious of how much it will cost them.
There is another perhaps more important aspect of this kind of tax that is perhaps even more attractive in an ideological way than the fact it is a pickpocket tax. It is a regressive tax. It is a tax that soaks the poor and middle income earners far more than the rich. It has none of the advantages of an income tax which can be so designed as to be fair. This tax inherently speaks to another characteristic of the Government and that is its refusal to be fair.
I do not want to be misunderstood that I am alleging only this Government as being sufficiently ideologically right wing as to see advantages of soaking the poor to pay for the rich. We have other examples, one revealed to us just recently. Colleagues of the Official Opposition in Ontario have demonstrated their capacity to respond to those ideological imperatives. They have lowered the corporate tax rate from 17 per cent to 15 per cent while raising the sales tax from 7 per cent to 8 per cent. It has to be admitted that that Government is a little less sneaky because at the provincial level everyone knows what they are paying. Nevertheless, the notion of fairness, whether it be the Ontario Government, the Saskatchewan Government or at the federal level, seems not to motivate the design of the tax structure.
April 21, 1988

The Government claims it has removed 850,000 people from the tax rolls while at the same time it does not mention that it was responsible for putting an additional million people on the tax rolls in the first place. We are dealing with a Government that, on the one hand, says it is interested in tax reform and, on the other hand, the average Canadian family is paying an additional $1,000 per year in federal taxes as a result of the Budgets of the present Government. Of course, while we would have to admit there are certain changes in the income tax structure which are beneficial to certain of our citizens, even those modest reforms are to be counteracted in the future by the national sales tax structure to be introduced, the details of which the Government has not seen fit to release, and I am sure they will reveal how unfair the approach of the Government will continue to be for ordinary Canadians.
There are a couple of aspects of the sales tax changes that I would like to examine for a moment. The 10 per cent increase in telecommunications and the effect it will have on our rural population, especially in northern Ontario, has already been adequately discussed. I would like to simply address two sales tax changes which are significant to my own constituency.
1 come from a community where automobile manufacture is extremely important. An important aspect of operating an automobile is economy. Since the Government has come into power, by virtue of steadily increasing sales taxes on gasoline, the average family is now spending $300 more a year on gasoline. It is a situation made worse by the progressive Liberals in Ontario who have themselves tacked on an additional one cent a litre tax on gasoline. So we have the pattern established of soaking the poor to benefit the rich, making it as difficult as possible for ordinary people. The significant issue, of course, is the prosperity of the automobile industry in Canada, severely threatened already. It is certainly not in the interests of that industry to impose an additional burden of cost of fuel on those who drive the cars that are manufactured so well in Windsor.
In Windsor, one of the more significant distilleries in the country, Hiram Walker, has been a corporate citizen of great value to our city. It employs a significant number of Windsor-ites who have been very worried for many years now about the steadily increasing burden of taxation on distilled spirits. One can look at this in two ways. I am fully conscious of the role the taxation of alcoholic beverages plays in trying to control the consumption of alcohol. Certainly there needs to be a control on the consumption of alcohol so that it is not abused. However, we go too far in limiting a perfectly legal product by
Excise Tax Act
means of a taxation regime which is costing jobs. The evidence is clear that the imbalanced imposition of sales taxes and excise taxes on distilled spirits is costing jobs. Distilled spirits are taxed more than beer and wine. The taxes should be balanced. This taxation really must stop in the interests of this industry and those constituents of mine who are constantly being threatened because jobs are being lost by the continued imposition of taxation on a product that is legal.
